item.title: Done Isn't Finished
item.description: Moving a climbing dome for the walnut brings an exposed plant circle into a new purpose of care, while the effects of both decisions remain open.
item.content:encoded:
Wednesday, November 11, 2026 · Black walnut · approximately 19 minutes 49 seconds recorded

Prompt

After I carry out an act of care, what can the changed place ask me to reconsider?

I came out with a prepared question about the difference between completing an action and fulfilling its purpose. Today there was a completed action to consider.

This is the fourth morning in a row that the climbing dome has been part of the sit. On November 8 I noticed it standing near an exposed root and wondered whether it belonged there. On November 9 I named an intention to move it for the walnut's sake and tried the structure to see whether I could shift it alone. On November 10 it was still where it had been, and I spent the morning asking how an intention can be definite while its future stays open. This morning I'm standing on the far side of the action, and that changes what I can ask. I'm looking at what I did, and at what it left.

Field Notes

The morning is sunny and chilly. More leaves lie beneath the walnut than remain on it. Most of the yellow still attached is on the lower limbs; higher branches open onto blue sky.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

November 11, earlier in the morning. Bare upper branches against blue sky, yellow foliage holding on the lower limbs at left, leaves across the ground, and the climbing dome at lower right in its new position. The view records the arrangement; it doesn't make the dome's old footprint legible.

I'm out later than usual again, and the light is already strong. Yesterday I was surprised by how quickly the lower canopy had opened. Today the surprise has settled into something closer to recognition: this is what the tree looks like now, and the yellow that's left won't be here long. A storm is forecast for the weekend, with cold behind it. That's a forecast, and I'm holding it as one.

Before recording, I moved the climbing dome about ten feet from its previous position. I had been considering that move for several days out of concern for the walnut, while wanting to preserve the structure's use for play. The move is complete. Whether it helps the tree remains unknown.

Where the dome stood, a ring of green plants surrounds a relatively bare center. I look at the leaves and soil and photograph the patch. Some foliage looks like what I have been calling lilyturf, but the identification remains provisional. The photograph records the arrangement without telling me everything living there or what each plant needs.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

November 11. Green groundcover around a relatively bare center, with fallen leaves across the patch, the walnut nearby and part of the relocated dome at left. The image does not establish species, root condition or the effects of the move.

I remember mowing around this area for about two years. I had chosen to leave the growth beneath the structure while the place continued to be used for play. I had also noticed the plants before. What surprised me now was having to consider their future after the move.

The circle, closer

The ring is roughly the size of the dome's footprint. The growth around its edge is low, maybe half a foot, narrow-leaved and dense enough to read as a band of green against the leaf litter. The center is different. A swing hung inside the dome, and two years of feet have worn the middle down. I called it a dry patch at first and then corrected myself while I was still looking: bare is what I can see. Whether it's dry is a claim about moisture, and I haven't put a hand to the soil.

I didn't move anything. I wanted a photograph of the arrangement before my own curiosity rearranged it.

The history matters here, and I got it partly wrong before I got it right. Nobody planted this as a patch. It also isn't ground that was simply left alone. I mowed around the dome on purpose, in part because the children wanted the plants under it kept, and they played there the whole time. So what I'm looking at is a place shaped by a play structure, a mower's path, a swing, small feet and a request... a used place with a history of selective restraint. Calling it untouched would flatter the story.

A word about names. In the recording I talk as though lilyturf and liriope were two candidates. They're the common and botanical names for the same genus. The question I left open on November 7 is still the open one: which species this is, and whether some of these clumps are a look-alike such as mondo grass. If it's liriope, it's most likely a planted ornamental that has wandered, and it may not be native here. I said out loud that caring for what's here doesn't require that it be what I'd have chosen. I still think that's right. It also doesn't settle what I should do if identification shows something that spreads at its neighbors' expense. The ivy on November 7 already taught me that a living plant's claim on my attention and a management decision are different questions.

I state a new commitment: leave this circle through winter. Concern for the plants and curiosity about what happens both enter that decision. Its future practice and effects will need their own record.

Reflection

Finishing the task

Moving the dome was a task I could finish in a morning. The good I hoped it might serve has a different measure. I cannot look at its new position and declare that the walnut has benefited. The tree continues through conditions and timescales that do not coincide with the end of my effort.

That difference is what I want “done isn't finished” to hold open. It does not mean that care can never succeed or that every purpose must continue indefinitely. It means that a successful movement and a good realized for another life are different things. Even a later change in the tree would need careful interpretation before I attributed it to this intervention.

I said this more boldly in the recording. I said that when an intention is for another living being, its fulfillment is kept by that being, and that I can complete the act without completing the intention. I want to keep the sentence and be careful with it. The walnut isn't withholding anything, and I'm not claiming that care can never arrive. What the sentence holds is an asymmetry of position. The moving was mine to do and mine to finish. Whether the ground over that root loosens, whether it mattered at all, belongs to a course of growth I don't run and can't hurry. I said it might show at next spring's leaf-out and then corrected myself: probably not then, probably years on, and even then tangled with drought, storms and everything else a tree lives through.

So there are at least three things where I'd been tempted to see one: the action, which is complete; the good it was for, which is open; and my knowledge of that good, which may stay partial even if the good is real.

A beneficiary I hadn't made room for

The plant circle makes a second difference concrete. I acted with the walnut in mind and found myself considering another beneficiary. My general concern for the yard's life was already present. What became more specific was what I now intend this patch to be for: a place where these plants can continue while I learn more about them.

I don't want to make that a story of suddenly discovering life I had never seen. Previous seeing had not led me to consider what would happen here after relocation. The action made a familiar feature practically significant in a different way. My prepared questions helped me articulate that response. So did memory, curiosity and prior commitments.

Seen, and not yet considered

Near the end of the sit I asked what I'd perceived that nothing I'd read predicted, and the answer that came was about me more than about the plants. I had seen this ring many times. I hadn't been blind to it. Yet across three days of planning the move I never once asked what would become of it. My care was aimed at the walnut's root, and that aim narrowed what counted as relevant. In a practical sense it did blind me, even while my eyes worked fine.

That's uncomfortable and useful. I've been arguing that another life's possible good can help specify what an act is for. This morning shows the other side of the same structure: a governing end also decides what drops out of consideration. An intention directed toward one beneficiary organizes a field of salience, and what falls outside it can be perfectly visible and still practically absent. The plants entered my purposes only when the completed action put a new question in front of me... what do I do with these now? Seeing was never the missing piece. Considering was.

I also need to correct something I said in the moment. I told the recorder that yesterday mowing meant keeping the yard even and safe to run on, and that this morning mowing this spot would mean mowing these plants. The second half is true. The first half tidies up the past. I had no settled plan to mow this circle yesterday; I'd been deliberately mowing around it for two years. What's new today is narrower and, I think, more interesting. The reason for leaving it has changed hands. It was left because a dome stood there and the children asked. Now the dome is gone, the old reason went with it, and I've had to decide whether the plants themselves are reason enough. I said they are, at least through the winter.

My reasons were mixed, and I said so at the time: the good of the soil, the good of these plants, a possible benefit to walnut roots that run under this ground, and plain curiosity about what happens. I also spoke of plant communication, intelligence and perhaps consciousness. Those are convictions and readings I carry with me. I didn't observe them in this ring this morning.

I gave myself a test as well. What would count against calling this a purpose I received from the place? If I'd have left the ring anyway because I like the look of a fairy ring in the yard, or because I didn't feel like mowing, or because it makes a good paragraph. I can't rule those out from inside the morning. I can check them against what I actually do when mowing starts again in March.

This is one way I am developing ecological intentionality. An end guides action, action alters a shared place, and attention to the affected lives can help specify a further end. The lives involved need not share my intentions. Their actual condition can still matter to what I intend next and to whether my response is adequate.

Shelter, and what the word can carry

In the recording I said that my care for the walnut took these plants' shelter away, and that I had four goods in front of me that don't add up to one: the walnut's root, this patch, the children's play, a tidy yard. I called it a real case of goods in conflict. Listening back, that's ahead of the evidence.

There are several possible goods here, but I have not demonstrated a necessary conflict between them. The dome's former position belonged to a pattern of avoiding the mower. Its removal changes that arrangement without proving injury to the plants. Leaving the ring may be compatible with the move. Calling the old arrangement shelter is a reason to investigate what it did, not an established account of its biological effects.

What I can say is that our purposes had effects we didn't aim at. A structure put up for play took part in these plants' situation for two years, and an act of care for a tree changed that situation in a morning. For months I've been saying that other lives can take part in what I intend without intending anything alongside me. Here the traffic runs the other way too. What I intend takes part in other lives whether or not I've thought about them. If that's right, being answerable has to cover what my purposes do as well as what they aim at.

Three sentences, said out loud

I ended by saying three sentences I might want in the paper, to hear whether I believed them.

First: when an intention is for another living being, I can finish the act and still not finish the intention; its fulfillment is kept in that life's own time. Standing there, this one felt closest to something I already knew from Stein's insistence that another's life is never given to me from the inside, and from Merleau-Ponty's gap. The research note below complicates how new it is.

Second: acting for one life can uncover another, and when it does, a new "for whom" can enter my ends that I didn't project and didn't choose. I said this one was good and that I had pushback of my own about it. The pushback is on the record above. "Uncover" overstates what happened to plants I'd already seen, and "didn't choose" sits oddly beside a decision I plainly made. What I didn't choose was the question.

Third: our purposes shelter and expose other lives without meaning to, so answerability has to cover what our ends do as well as what they aim at. I said this was the strongest of the three, and after the corrections I still think so. It asks the least of the evidence and the most of me.

Remainder belongs within this care. I can identify more, observe longer and make a definite commitment without becoming the author of these lives or their future.

Research Connection

Edith Stein gives the distinction between intention and realized benefit a substantial predecessor. In Finite and Eternal Being V §§16–17, especially pp. 313–316 in Kurt F. Reinhardt's translation, she separates knowing a possible good from its actual realization in the beneficiary. Selected primary passages were checked after the sit. My developing extension concerns how the aftermath of one action can bring another beneficiary into the purpose of a subsequent act.

During the sit I reached for Aristotle's remark that "that for the sake of which" is twofold (τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα; De Anima II.4, 415b2–3, repeated at 415b20–21). On the long-standing reading he's distinguishing the aim of an act from the one for whom it's done, the οὗ from the ᾧ, and J. A. Smith's translation renders it that way. That gave me a compact way to say what changed at the circle: the aim of my yard work didn't need to change for a new "for whom" to enter it. Two cautions. The passage belongs to a discussion of nutrition and reproduction, and it makes no argument about what I owe a patch of groundcover. And the traditional reading has been challenged in recent scholarship, so I should cite it as the common interpretation and check the Greek against a critical edition before leaning on it in the paper.

Husserl's accounts of motivation and practical possibility remain a serious explanation of this sequence. Prepared language, memory and valued ends help make the response intelligible. The ecological proposal concerns the work done by independent living beneficiaries within that explanation; this case does not establish a new basic form of conscious activity.

I also owe Husserl a correction. In the recording I said he gives me fulfillment as the moment an empty intention meets what it meant. That's too quick, and the quickness flatters my own claim. His account of fulfillment is graded and temporal, and his lectures on willing describe an action as fulfilled progressively, phase by phase, as it's carried out. Discussions of those lectures in The Routledge Handbook of Phenomenology of Agency (2021) also distinguish the will at work in a present action from a resolve directed at a future end. That distinction fits this morning closely. Dragging the dome fulfilled the will to move it, in the doing. The resolve it served, an arrangement of this yard that's good for the walnut and still good for play, reaches past the action and remains unfulfilled. So "done isn't finished" is something Husserl can already say. What I'm adding, if I'm adding anything, concerns where the fulfilling evidence would have to come from: a continuing life that isn't mine. These are selected passages read after the sit, and I haven't worked through the lectures themselves.

The theological reflection turns to Leviticus 25. Land sabbath suggests a practiced limit on possession. My winter commitment is an analogy requiring further thought, not an instance of the chapter's agrarian institution. Its social exclusions also complicate any easy appeal to universal shared rest.

The detail that caught me is a single word. In the Greek of Leviticus 25:5, what the land produces during its sabbath is τὰ αὐτόματα ἀναβαίνοντα, the things that come up of themselves (αὐτόματος, "self-moved, of its own accord"; the phrase returns at 25:11). In the growing-seed parable I read here yesterday, Mark writes αὐτομάτη ἡ γῆ καρποφορεῖ, "of itself the earth bears fruit" (4:28). I checked both in online texts of the Septuagint and the Greek New Testament after the sit; they haven't been collated against the printed critical editions. I wondered aloud whether Mark had Leviticus in mind. I can't claim that. A shared word shows a shared vocabulary for growth that nobody engineered. Dependence would need its own evidence.

In the recording I called this circle a fallow we kept by accident. The phrase is half right. The rest wasn't accidental, since I chose not to mow there, and it wasn't rest from human presence, since the children were in it constantly. But Leviticus doesn't imagine an empty field either. During the land's sabbath its yield is food for the household and its slaves, hired and bound laborers, the livestock and the wild animals (25:6–7). The rest it describes is a limit on sowing, pruning and reaping as one's own, within a place that stays inhabited. Read that way, a ring of plants that came through two years of play is closer to the text than my word "accident" suggested. And the chapter's reason for the limit is a claim about ownership: "the land is mine," with the people as προσήλυτοι καὶ πάροικοι, strangers and sojourners (25:23; πάροικος, a resident without a citizen's title).

Moltmann is the reading-list voice I need here. In God in Creation, chapter XI, he treats the sabbath as the completion of creation and reads the sabbath year of Leviticus 25 as evidence that the feast belongs to the land and to the other creatures as well as to people. That gives the winter commitment a theological horizon larger than my yard without making my yard an instance of it. It also sharpens what's missing. Sabbath in that chapter is communal and scheduled. One person deciding to leave a circle unmowed is, at most, a private rehearsal of the posture.

For the Ecology of the Cross, I propose that participation in Christ can form communities willing to reconsider their purposes in light of affected lives. Colossians 1:15–20, considered separately after the sit, supplies the Christological starting point. The extension into communal ecological responsibility requires argument and actual communal evidence. An imposed cost does not become redemptive because the person imposing it intended care.

I said one more thing at the tree that I want to keep on the record with its limits. I said a cruciform care doesn't wait until it can be innocent: it acts, it looks at what the act uncovered, and it stays. The staying is the part I can stand behind this morning. I moved the dome for one creature's sake, the move changed things for others, and I'm answerable for both. Whether "cruciform" is the right word for that answerability is a theological claim I haven't yet argued. It would need more than my willingness to keep looking, and it can't be allowed to turn somebody else's loss into my offering.

A congregation could begin with a concrete inquiry before changing its grounds: what is already living here, what practices have shaped the place, and whose needs have not yet entered the proposal? Answering would involve people who use and maintain the site as well as ecological investigation. That is a possible shared undertaking, not an outcome established by this backyard encounter.

The question I'd carry to such a conversation came out plainly at the tree. Communities set things down for good reasons: a parking lot, a fence, a playground, a mowing schedule. Things grow up under and around them that nobody decided on. Then something gets moved, for another good reason, and what it was covering comes to light. What's been living under the things we put down for other purposes, and who finds out when we move them? I can't answer that for any congregation from my backyard. I can listen for it.

Source and publication notes

The prepared seed for this sit already contained the three sentences, the fallow analogy, the Aristotle reference and the proposed winter commitment. Their appearance in the recording is not independent evidence for them. What the recording added on its own: the definite statement of the commitment, the mixed reasons for it, the memory of deliberately mowing around the dome at the children's request, the correction from "dry" to "bare," and the admission that the plants had been seen before.

The relocation was carried out earlier the same morning and is reported, not recorded. The winter commitment is prospective; I plan to return to it when mowing resumes in March 2027. Plant identification is provisional. No root condition, soil compaction, microclimate or benefit to the walnut has been assessed.

Weather details beyond what I could feel and see come from a forecast. The Stein, Husserl, Moltmann and Colossians material entered through source review after the sit. Aristotle, Leviticus 25 and the comparison with Mark 4 were part of the prepared seed and the recording; the Greek wording was checked afterward in online texts only.

Question Carried Forward

When I return to this circle, what would show that the plants' continuing lives guide my commitment, and what evidence would ask me to change course?

item.title: A Future Not Mine Alone
item.description: A thinner canopy unsettles an expected timetable and opens a question about intentions whose futures remain answerable to independent life.
item.content:encoded:
Tuesday, November 10, 2026 · Black walnut · approximately 17½ minutes recorded

Prompt

How can I intend a future while remaining open to what the lives involved may require of it?

I came out with that question already in mind. Yesterday I had described a possible act of care and tested whether I could carry it out. Today I wanted to ask what remains open even after I can name an intention and believe myself capable of acting on it.

Field Notes

I'm at the walnut later than usual. The sun is higher and brighter, with shadows in different places. Construction work and passing cars reach the yard. There are a few clouds, and the morning still feels chilly.

The lower canopy looks much thinner than I expected. I knew the leaves were going, but I had imagined another week or two with some yellow foliage remaining. There are many more leaves on the ground than on the tree now. The change feels faster than the future I had pictured.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

November 10. Exposed upper branches, remaining yellow foliage, bright sunlight and fallen leaves beneath the walnut. The dome stands at the right. This view records the morning's arrangement; it does not establish how much fell overnight or what caused the change.

Yesterday's canopy and gusts belong to memory. I connect the thinner foliage with that wind, but I did not watch the overnight sequence. The open branches are here now; their recent history requires more than this view.

The climbing dome remains where it was. I have not relocated it since yesterday's recording. I still intend to move it and have another position in mind, but I have not established that its present location harms the walnut or that the alternative would help. Shade, play and the tree's possible good all belong to the question.

Reflection

When I expect a change but not its pace

I want to be careful about how I describe being surprised. Yesterday I already suspected that the tree might lose its leaves quickly. I remembered gusts coming through, and I knew we were entering the part of November when the walnut might become nearly bare. I was anticipating the change. Yet I still wasn't ready for quite this much opening in the lower canopy.

So this isn't a story in which I confidently predicted one thing and the tree proved me wrong. My expectation was broad enough to include faster leaf loss, but the degree and timing of the change exceeded the picture I had been carrying. I can recognize that the canopy looks different today while admitting that I didn't watch the interval in which the change happened.

That seems worth describing in its own right. I don't encounter the walnut in a succession of isolated snapshots. Yesterday's canopy is retained in memory, today's appearance is in front of me, and I'm already wondering what the tree will look like in another few days. The present encounter has a past and a future within it. But neither my recollection nor my anticipation contains the walnut's actual course of development.

I'm interested in this because it gives me a modest example of being affected while I am consciously directed toward something. I came outside with questions about purpose and future possibility. A visible difference I hadn't fully anticipated interrupted those questions and made me consider the time of the tree's own ongoing life. That wasn't a new ethical decision or a completed change of intention. It was a particular way in which the world entered the present direction of my consciousness.

The canopy has unsettled a more specific expectation about timing. That is different from changing what I intend to do for the walnut.

I still have the same proposed move in view. What has become clearer is that carrying it out would not settle the future I hope it might serve. A new location could solve one problem and create another. Better evidence might favor leaving the structure alone. The walnut would continue living through either decision, with consequences I cannot declare good simply because I meant well.

An intention can be definite without containing a finished picture of its fulfillment. I can be directed toward a shared arrangement that supports play and takes the walnut's life seriously, while remaining uncertain about what that arrangement requires. The uncertainty gives me reasons to investigate, consider alternatives and return to the effects of what I do.

But I need to distinguish kinds of revision. Choosing a better location could change the means while preserving the same purpose. Learning that my idea of a good arrangement excludes important lives or needs could require reconsidering the purpose itself. Today's canopy changes my expectation about leaf loss. It does not by itself establish either practical revision.

A future I can intend without possessing

The dome brings the problem into a more deliberate practical situation. Yesterday I tested whether I could move it and decided that I probably could. Today it is still in the same place. The capacity to do something has not settled what I should do or what the result would mean for the tree.

I placed the dome where it was useful for shade and play. Those goods didn't disappear when I began worrying about a nearby root. Now I'm considering a different arrangement, possibly farther into the yard, in which the children's play and the walnut's possible good can both matter. I haven't established that the present dome position injures a root or that another position will improve the tree's condition.

What is the intention here? It isn't exhausted by pushing a structure from one place to another. I'm intending a possible future of this shared yard. That future remains definite enough to guide inquiry and action, yet open enough to let what I discover about the actual place matter.

Suppose I learn that the dome is doing no harm, that moving it would disturb another area, or that there is a better way to protect a root while preserving play. Those findings might change the means. But there is also a deeper possibility: they might change what I mean by making a good place for my family and the walnut. I don't have to claim that such a deeper revision happened this morning to begin developing the philosophical account of how it could occur.

That distinction helps me say something positive about Ecological Intentionality. Another being's possible future may matter within the direction of an intention now. Its life need not wait until afterward to become a standard by which I judge success. What I understand myself to be doing can already depend on whom I seek to benefit and what I am prepared to reconsider for that being's sake.

This is also why remainder belongs within the relationship. Familiarity makes my concern more particular. It does not make the walnut's future mine to compose. Some unknowns can become clearer through inquiry; greater knowledge still leaves a continuing life beyond my project.

Reception, directedness, and an unfinished good

I keep returning to a sentence from our recent work: the world is not only what consciousness is directed toward. Its independent lives and processes may participate in the very directedness of consciousness, even while remaining irreducibly other.

What does that mean in an ordinary encounter? At least it means I can discover that the purpose I brought with me isn't as self-contained as I assumed. I may have intended a convenient use of the yard, and then begun to intend a shared place in which another living being's possible good helps determine what I take a successful use to be. The possibility arises through repeated encounters, observation, practical experience, reading, memory, and further inquiry. I can't isolate one moment and call it the entire cause.

But I also don't want to define ecological intentionality as a history of learning. This morning's encounter matters now. I'm actively directed toward a future, with remembered experiences behind me and unfolding lives around me. Some of what matters to that direction has been given through a relationship I neither created nor fully control.

Perhaps receptivity is one way that an intention can be fully an intention. I can commit to a purpose without having every condition of its fulfillment settled in advance. Being open to correction doesn't mean that I am not directed. It can mean that what I'm directed toward is another life whose future won't coincide exactly with my plans.

And the remainder isn't just a blank space in my knowledge. The walnut remains a living being with its own ongoing possibilities even as I study its roots, leaves, bark, soil and neighbors more closely. I become involved with it, perhaps more intimate with it, without becoming the author of what it is.

I think that's what intimacy with remainder begins to name. The relationship can make my purposes more particular and more responsible while allowing the other to remain other.

An actual future and a communal one

There's a related question I've been carrying through my years of church and classroom work. Groups of people don't always decide from scratch what they're for. Congregations form shared expectations through worship, memories, traditions, buildings, budgets, habits and teaching. Those expectations make some future possibilities seem obvious and leave others almost invisible.

When a congregation decides what its property should become, it can bring those familiar purposes to the land. But the water moving across the property, the trees and soil, the people who work there, the neighboring households and other living beings have their own histories and possibilities. What if sustained relationships with that place begin to change what the congregation understands itself to be directed toward?

That's not a claim that churches are one enormous individual consciousness, or that a congregation's plan has already been transformed by a watershed. I want to investigate how a genuine communal we can develop a shared direction through the activity and differences of its members, and how the nonhuman lives of a place might participate in specifying that direction without being members who vote or assent.

The question is not only how to make a preexisting church project greener. It is whether the relationship with a place might change what a congregation understands the project, or its common life, to be for.

Research Connection

The philosophical proposal is that ecological relations can help specify and revise conscious ends. Today's case contributes a narrower distinction: corrected anticipation, a continuing practical intention, an action still ahead, and consequences still unknown. Whether the living relation also helps constitute the conscious act requires further argument.

Husserl gives part of this account an existing foundation. A selected primary passage in Ideas II §60(a) describes practical possibility through experienced capability. The earlier trial concerns what I think I can do. It does not settle what I intend the action for or whether that purpose will be adequately served. Ordinary motivated deliberation remains a serious explanation of the sequence.

What the philosophers contribute to today's question

This encounter doesn't require me to begin by finding a fault in phenomenology. Husserl has serious resources for describing how anticipation is fulfilled or disappointed, how an embodied person comes to experience what they can do, and how practical life is motivated by a meaningful surrounding world. My changed image of the canopy and the still-uncompleted dome project can both be described through those resources.

Edith Stein's account of non-primordiality helps me take another's life seriously without treating it as something I experience from within. Merleau-Ponty's investigations of bodily involvement and noncoincidence open a different conversation about being intertwined with a world that remains other. Neither approach needs to be declared inadequate before I can ask what their resources make possible when the independent lives and possible goods of other beings become central to the formation of an intended end.

The additional question I'm constructing is how reception through ecological relationship enters what consciousness, individually and together, is for. I want that to become a positive account with its own explanations and consequences, not another list of things our predecessors left out.

The theological question has another starting point. Mark 4:26–29 places sowing and harvesting alongside growth the sower does not fully understand. I read this kingdom parable as an opening toward responsible participation without ownership of the whole future.

For the Ecology of the Cross, I want to develop the claim that participation in Christ can form a congregation's purposes in relation to lives it cannot possess. Colossians 1:15–20, considered after the sit, connects creation, church, resurrection and reconciliation through the cross. The ecological extension needs its own argument; neither passage supplies a grounds-management plan.

Sowing, growth, and the life that continues

I was interested in Mark 4:26–29 this morning because the person sowing is genuinely involved in an unfolding future without producing that future by an act of will. The person scatters seed, sleeps and rises, sees growth beyond their own understanding, and later harvests. The earth's activity is not an instruction to stop working. Human action and processes beyond human control both belong to the story.

This is a parable of the kingdom of God. I shouldn't turn it into a direct teaching on the physiology of walnut leaves or a ready-made model of environmental management. But it makes me want to ask whether Christian participation can include a way of acting that is neither withdrawal nor mastery. What if a community can intend, act, return, investigate and revise while understanding that it does not possess the whole future toward which it is directed?

That is a constructive theological question. The Ecology of the Cross will have to say more about Christ, creatureliness, participation, institutions and whose suffering is involved than this one parable can establish.

A congregation might begin by asking how to improve its property, then come to reconsider what kind of shared place it seeks to sustain. That possibility concerns a real communal “we,” formed through deliberation, disagreement and practice. It is a proposed inquiry, not a reported church outcome. It would require ecological knowledge, attention to the people doing the work, and a history of the place. Calling a project sacrificial would never make costs imposed on others redemptive.

Source and publication notes

The forecast and lunar details belong to the private preparation, not to direct measurement here. The biblical reflection on Mark 4:26–29 was included in the prepared seed and spoken during the sit. The comparison with Colossians 1:15–20 was added during the subsequent source review, not presented as something discovered in the recording.

For the phenomenological comparison, the primary working reference is Husserl's Ideas II, §60(a), on practical ability. A related scholarly interlocutor is James Jardine, *Empathy, Embodiment, and the Person* (2022), especially chapters 4 and 6, on nature as a source of motivation and the distinction between practical value, decision and bodily action. item.title: Directed Through This World
item.description: A practical trial beside the walnut separates what I can do from what I intend it for, while the tree's continuing life keeps that purpose open to correction.
item.content:encoded:
Monday, November 9, 2026 · Black walnut · approximately 24 minutes recorded

Prompt

What am I directed toward, and what does this independently living relation contribute to the direction of that intention?

I came to the walnut with a working proposal: consciousness can receive direction through relationships with lives and places it does not author. This morning I wanted to describe one actual intention through which to develop that thought.

Field Notes

The sky is blue, sunlight comes through the walnut, and the cold is something I feel on my skin. There is little breeze. Bird calls mingle with construction noise and passing cars.

The upper branches are almost bare. Yellow foliage remains lower down, while the ground holds brown fallen material with fresher yellow pieces above it. During the sit I watch a couple of leaves detach and fall. Yesterday afternoon's unexpectedly open canopy remains in memory beside what I see now.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

November 9. Exposed upper branches, remaining yellow foliage, sunlight through a lower branch and fallen material beneath the walnut. The climbing dome appears at the right; the photograph records placement, not its effects on the tree.

The dome stands near a visible root. I have tried moving it enough to think I could relocate it, and I have a possible alternative position in mind. I still have not completed that relocation or established that the present arrangement harms the walnut.

Later, I find myself looking at the bark. The surface holds my attention while the processes I understand to continue within the tree remain unavailable to this immediate view.

There are other things in this morning's field besides the tree. I hear calls that I take to be thrashers and Carolina wrens, nearby construction, and traffic. I notice how the position of the morning sunlight seems different from other mornings when I've stood in this spot. Part of that comparison comes from memory, not from measuring the sun's position today. The sky and the sounds matter, too. This is an ordinary yard amid other human projects, not an isolated philosophical experiment.

A practical trial before I began speaking

I should be clear about the sequence of the dome decision. Yesterday I was already considering moving the climbing dome, partly because I had begun noticing a root near it. Overnight I continued thinking about it, and before this morning's recording I tried the structure enough to see whether I could move it myself. That trial made relocation feel possible. It did not establish that I had found the right new place or that the tree needed the structure moved.

I also took a photograph of the root and dome together. I'm considering a position perhaps ten feet farther toward the middle of the yard. That distance is my provisional idea, not a conclusion from a root-health assessment. The dome has been a place of shade and play for the children, so this isn't a situation in which the human purpose was worthless and the walnut's purpose was automatically right. Several goods belong to the arrangement.

I can now say more confidently that moving the dome is something I think I can do. Whether moving it is something I ought to do, and what would actually serve the walnut's continuing life, are separate questions. Nothing in this recording establishes that I carried out the move.

Reflection

What the intended move is for

The dome was placed here for shade and play. Those remain good purposes. Now the walnut's possible good enters my intention for the arrangement as well. I want continued use of the space to be answerable to this tree's life.

That gives the philosophical proposal something specific to explain. The walnut is more than the object I happen to look at while considering an already fixed project. My relation with it may help specify the future I am trying to bring about: what I hope to sustain, whose good matters within that hope, and what could make the proposed action a mistake.

The relation includes returning, remembering, reading and thinking overnight. Those mediations do not make the concern unreal. They do mean that I cannot attribute the whole intention to an isolated moment of seeing a root.

Trying the dome adds another element. A possible project becomes something I think I can undertake. But the trial answers a question about ability. It does not establish that relocation would help the tree, or show that my purpose changed while I tested the structure.

I can therefore carry a definite intention without making movement itself the measure of success. If better evidence favored leaving the dome where it is, care for the walnut could require a different means. If I remained determined to move it regardless of what I learned, I would need to reconsider my account of what the action was for.

The ability isn't the purpose

There's a distinction here that feels small until I try to describe the conscious act itself. I didn't go outside this morning with the sole aim of discovering whether a metal and plastic structure could be moved. I went out with a concern about the walnut and about the family's use of this space. When I tested the dome, I learned something about the means available to me. But my intention to do something for the walnut's possible good was already in play.

So what am I actually directed toward? Not only a dome, a root or a position ten feet away. I'm directed toward a possible future arrangement in which play continues and I have reason to think I'm not imposing unnecessary costs on this living tree. The walnut's good is something I mean within the project, although I haven't yet established what that good requires in this particular situation.

This is what I wanted to explore last night with the language of received directedness. Perhaps another life can participate in specifying what my intention is for, rather than being added to a project whose purpose was fixed in advance.

I need to be able to say what could prove my choice mistaken. If I learn that the dome's present position is harmless and that moving it would damage something else, the same concern for the walnut might require me to do nothing. If I insist on moving it no matter what I learn, I would have good reason to reconsider whether this is genuinely a walnut-answerable intention. Caring about another being doesn't mean I get to make my proposal immune to that being's reality.

This doesn't establish a new category of intentionality. It gives me a particular act to describe: an end that I can name, a bodily possibility I tested, an action still projected, and a standard of success that is not mine to declare fulfilled.

The tree doesn't deliver a parable

About halfway through the sit, I found myself comparing this relationship to the way a parable can unsettle a listener. I love the Good Samaritan and the prodigal son partly because they aren't flat instructions. You can return to the same story and be challenged in a different way because of who you are and what you're bringing to it.

I don't mean that the walnut is telling me a story or preaching at me. It isn't secretly giving me a command about my yard. Rather, the relationship keeps disturbing the questions I thought I had already settled. I'm out here with one purpose, and something about this actual place can make me ask what that purpose is for. The parable is my interpretive comparison, not evidence that the tree has composed one.

That distinction matters. A metaphor may help me notice a genuine interruption, but it doesn't prove what produced the interruption or what another being intends.

Nearness that leaves a remainder

Looking at bark is another act. Here I am trying to understand something about a life whose surface is available and whose continuing processes exceed what I can watch this morning.

Some of what I cannot see could become better known through biological inquiry. That is different from claiming access to the tree's experience. And neither more information nor greater familiarity would make its life coincide with mine.

This is what I mean by intimacy with remainder: a relation can become more particular and more consequential while the other remains independent. Its possible good can matter within my intention without being exhausted by what I currently believe that good to be.

A stronger claim I still want to investigate

I also said something more speculative aloud today. I suspect that trees and other living beings, and perhaps the material relationships of rivers, rocks and soil, involve forms of conscious activity that we humans are inclined to overlook. That's a metaphysical position I want to take seriously enough to investigate, not something I observed directly by standing beneath a black walnut for twenty-four minutes.

I don't mean that a rock, a river, a walnut and a human being necessarily possess the same sort of inner life. Some of these are organisms; some are material formations or relations that include living and nonliving processes. Nor does reciprocal influence by itself prove that the other side of the relationship intends me as I intend it.

What today's encounter can establish is narrower, and perhaps more useful for the present paper. I'm involved with a living being whose ongoing activity I don't author. My conscious project is beginning to include what I understand as that being's possible good. I'm trying to discover what it would mean for that good to participate in the direction of the intention, rather than enter only afterward as an external ethical test.

This is precisely where intimacy with remainder becomes something more than a description of uncertainty. The closer I become to the walnut and the more concrete my purposes become, the more important it is that the tree is not exhausted by my description of it. Some of what I don't know is researchable. Otherness doesn't disappear when those facts become clearer.

Research Connection

The positive account of Ecological Intentionality now has three distinguishable moments to work with: a relation helps specify an intended end; practical exploration makes a means available; further encounter and inquiry can correct the project. These moments overlap in experience, but their evidence differs. A reported trial is not a completed relocation, and a completed relocation would still require an account of its consequences.

Husserl helps make the middle moment precise. In a selected passage from Ideas II §60, practical possibility concerns what the subject experiences as within their capability. That offers a strong account of why trying the dome changes what I can envisage doing. His existing account of motivation also challenges any suggestion that phenomenology knows only a passive spectator. The unresolved question is what the living relation contributes to specifying the end of this present intention. Today's case develops that question without demonstrating a new basic structure of consciousness.

The congregational question begins from a different warrant. Psalm 104:10–24 places human activity among springs, trees, habitats and other creatures' rhythms. I read this as an invitation to understand human purposes within a world whose provision exceeds our use of it.

For the Ecology of the Cross, I propose that participation in Christ can form a communal “we” whose mission remains receptive to fellow creatures. Colossians 1:15–20 connects creation, the church, resurrection and reconciliation through the cross. Extending that confession into ecological communal discernment is an argument to develop, not a decision procedure stated in the passage.

A congregation might begin a grounds decision by asking how to maintain its property, then discover reasons to reconsider what that property serves. A real case would need ecological knowledge, the history of the place, participation from affected people and evidence of what the community actually changes. It would also have to ask who bears the costs. Calling a decision sacrificial cannot make imposed injury good.

A communal direction that can be received

This is something I don't want to put off until a final application section of the dissertation. I've spent much of my adult life among congregations and people trying to work out what a community is supposed to do. Shared purposes can genuinely form us, but they can also narrow what we regard as possible or important. We can become very good at preserving a mission without asking whether our understanding of it needs to change.

I keep wondering whether the actual lives of a congregation's place can enter that shared directedness. Not as a nature-themed addition to an established ministry, but as part of what helps a community understand its own purposes differently. We might become capable of consciously intending a future together that we weren't able to articulate before a relationship with that place began to change us.

Psalm 104 is interesting to me because its creaturely world is not arranged around a church's usefulness. In the passage I considered this morning, springs give drink to wild animals, birds have nesting places, trees are watered, mountain goats have their heights, and rocks shelter other creatures. Human work appears within that differentiated world in verse 23, not as the exclusive reason the world exists. That's not yet an ecclesiology, but it is a compelling place to ask about receiving a purpose within a creation that exceeds our purposes.

For the Ecology of the Cross, I want something more particular than a call to appreciate interconnection. What does participation in Christ do to a community's shared direction? How might that participation form a we whose understanding of mission can still be corrected by lives we don't own and can't fully represent? Those questions require Christian theological argument and real congregational practice. Today's walnut encounter gives me a way to state them, not the authority to announce that a church has already answered them.

What I can and cannot claim from today

This morning gives me a reported practical trial and a presently stated intention. It doesn't give me a completed relocation, a diagnosis of root injury, an ecological success measurement, evidence that the walnut consciously intended anything toward me, or proof that Husserl's account has failed.

It also gives me two different acts that I don't want to combine. Testing a dome concerns a possible action and its beneficiary. Looking at bark concerns knowing and encountering a continuing life that exceeds my present view. Both matter to the larger question of how directed consciousness can be received and redirected, but they aren't the same event.

The script I brought outside supplied some of today's language in advance. Books, previous encounters, family purposes and last night's writing are all part of the mediation. The distinctive event in the record is that I had already tried the dome and could now describe a more actionable intention. That may be modest, but it's enough to carry into the paper.

Sources and limits

The selected textual comparison is **Edmund Husserl, Ideas II, §60(a), in the Richard Rojcewicz and André Schuwer translation (Kluwer, 1989), on experienced practical possibility and the "I can." This is a section-level reference, not a newly page-checked direct quotation. James Jardine, Empathy, Embodiment, and the Person (Springer, 2022), especially chapter 4, §4.4, and chapter 6, §§6.1.2 and 6.3**, provides further resources for how worldly circumstances motivate valuation, action, agency and habituality. I'm treating those as close-reading targets for the constructive draft, not as arguments I have already settled.

The Psalm 104:10–24 reflection was part of the morning sit. The Colossians 1:15–20 comparison was added during the post-sit source review. Both links use the NRSVUE English translation; neither comparison is offered as a completed historical-critical or ecological argument.

Question Carried Forward

How does this independent life enter what I am presently trying to do, and what evidence could change the end itself rather than only the means I choose?

item.title: What This Life Makes Possible
item.description: Leaving the leaves and reconsidering a climbing dome make the ecological formation of practical purposes more concrete, while Philippians 2 opens a separate question about communal life.
item.content:encoded:
Sunday, November 8, 2026 · Black walnut · approximately 53 minutes recorded

Prompt

What has this relationship made possible for me to notice, understand or intend that wasn't available to me in the same way when I began? And what actually brought about those changes?

That is the positive question I want to begin with now. The work has become more than learning to distinguish a present appearance from a memory or inference, although that discipline still matters. I want to understand how repeated encounters with a continuing life have helped form the questions I can ask and the practical purposes I can undertake.

The walnut does not have to provide an insight this morning. An ordinary day could still belong to that history.

Field Notes

The sky is blue and the sun is out. The air feels crisp and chilly, different from the damp cold of the preceding mornings. Light comes through a neighboring maple and across the yard toward the walnut. I see wrens, report crows passing overhead, and hear acorns falling from the oaks.

Fresh yellow leaves lie above brown and darker litter. Looking back toward the whole tree, I find long stretches of exposed upper branches with foliage remaining farther down. I recognize the difference through earlier visits and photographs. That history helps me see change without letting me witness all the events between the views.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

November 8. Sunshine through the walnut's branches, remaining yellow foliage, and a ground covered with fallen material. The view records this morning's arrangement; it does not establish the causes or timing of each change.

I meant to consider a branch that I remembered carrying leaves yesterday. Instead, the plants at the trunk drew my attention down. Standing between the fence and the walnut, I looked at the ivy, violet-like leaves and lilyturf, then outward across the litter. I stepped back for the whole-tree view and returned to the same patch.

Yesterday's identification work is part of why these plants now catch my eye. I have become more confident through photographs and field guides, although I still owe the record the diagnostic traits and exact sources. I can describe a vine climbing the base and the mixed foliage around it. Whether these plants help or harm one another requires further investigation.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

The trunk base and its living setting, November 8. Ivy-like foliage, narrow clumps, broader leaves and yellow-brown litter occupy the foreground. The photograph gives context and placement, not a diagnosis of ecological benefit or injury.

Reflection

What returning has made possible

When I began this practice, I did not have the same questions about the ground beneath the walnut, the organisms that might use its leaves, or the placement of things near its roots. The tree had not been absent from my life. My ways of attending and deciding were less particular.

Its changing appearance matters to that development. So do the discipline of returning, the books I read, my earlier purposes, affection and memory. I don't think those mediations automatically compete with the relationship. Reading can be one way an encounter continues: something in the yard prompts a question, the question takes me to a source, and what I learn changes how I approach the yard again.

The walnut's contribution need not be unique to this walnut to be real. Other trees lose leaves and expose branches. This tree does so here, through a life with which I have this history of encounters. The inquiry concerns that particular contribution without making it the sole cause of what follows.

My positive proposal is that a sustained relationship with an independently living being can help form the repertoire of questions and purposes through which I act. The subject doing the noticing has a history, too. What I can notice as a practical problem has developed through the relation.

What happens when a book interrupts me?

A second, quite different kind of interruption happened yesterday. I picked up Joseph Campbell's The Flight of the Wild Gander again and found myself reading about the Brothers Grimm, Clemens Brentano and Achim von Arnim. A name leapt off the page. Was this Clemens Brentano connected to the Franz Brentano who has been following me through so much of the intentionality question?

I went looking. The family connection really is there: the Romantic poet Clemens was Franz Brentano's uncle. It was one of those delightful moments when something I was reading for pleasure unexpectedly returned me to an academic question. I hadn't gone looking for another phenomenological connection. The association redirected what I wanted to investigate.

But that episode is also a helpful check on the philosophical story I might tell about the walnut. A text can change the trajectory of my attention. A remembered name can become suddenly salient. A conversation with another person, a book, or an artifact can alter what I expect to find next. I wouldn't want to attribute that little discovery directly to the walnut's biological activity. The exact Campbell passage and page still need checking in the physical copy, so I'm treating this as an episode of my own reading rather than offering Campbell as a verified philosophical authority here.

What, then, is the difference between the formative history of a text and that of a living organism? I can't answer that by saying only living things surprise me. They clearly don't. Nor can I say that reading is merely a distraction from the living relation. When a book helps me understand what might be happening in the leaf litter, the reading may become one of the ways I respond to this actual place. The question is whether the learning remains answerable to the specific lives here, rather than making them illustrations of something I read elsewhere.

I also found myself thinking about Ursula K. Le Guin's Always Coming Home. It's a fictional work that asks me to inhabit forms of cultural attention very different from my own. It can unsettle what I take for granted about place, use and naming. But fiction is not an ethnographic report about an actual Indigenous people, any more than a fictional dinosaur is a living animal. Its imaginative power gives me questions to carry back to the world, not evidence that those questions have been answered.

These interruptions matter because the history I'm trying to understand extends well beyond my morning seat. Yet the distinctions matter just as much: a work of fiction, a historical book, another person's question, and a growing walnut do not contribute to my intentional life in exactly the same way.

The leaves: a plan with reported follow-through

The sequence of the leaf decision remains important. Questions about fallen material led to ecological reading. That reading contributed to my decision to leave whole leaves rather than repeat the planned mowing. By November 6 I was already reporting the revision; that morning's squirrels and falling leaf did not cause a decision made earlier.

Yesterday I also corrected the account of the original plan. I had been thinking about soil care and safe use of the yard as well as tidiness. The comparison was never simply between one selfish purpose and one ecological purpose. Several goods were already involved.

Today I can add something small but concrete: I have left the leaves uncollected since yesterday, as I intended. That is a report of follow-through over a bounded interval. It does not show which organisms are using the litter or establish that the decision has benefited them. I want those differences to remain visible: an intention, its implementation and its effects are three parts of the story.

A new question beside an exposed root

Another practical possibility emerged more clearly during the recording. The climbing dome stands near an exposed walnut root. I estimated the visible root to be about a foot from the structure and began describing an intention to investigate moving the dome over winter.

I originally valued shade and a place for play. Those purposes still matter. Now I also ask what the placement means for the tree's continuing life. The root did not become important only because I learned a new philosophical word. Repeated attention and a growing concern for this particular tree have made the arrangement something I need to reconsider.

I have not established that the dome is damaging the root, moved the structure, or selected a verified better location. The alternatives I mention are possibilities. The next step is to record the current arrangement, its uses, what evidence is needed, and what could make me revise the plan. A location without visible roots would not by itself settle the condition of what lies below ground.

The practical purpose is becoming more specific before its outcome is known.

The measure of care cannot be my intention alone

I keep coming back to the difference between having a purpose and realizing a good. If I decide to move the dome, I could be acting out of concern for the walnut while still making an ecologically uninformed choice. The new position could be worse for the tree, less useful for the children, or inconvenient for ordinary movement through the yard. A place where I see no exposed roots is not necessarily free of roots beneath the ground.

Likewise, retaining whole leaves may be a reasonable response to what I've learned about overwintering habitat. But I don't yet know which creatures are in this litter, how its particular distribution matters to them, or whether an arrangement that helps one group creates a problem for another. I can document the action or the restraint. I cannot infer its full consequences from my reason for choosing it.

There is a useful tension here. If I insist on waiting until I have complete knowledge, I might never act. If I treat every compassionate purpose as sufficient, I can easily mistake goodwill for adequate care. The discipline I'm after is something between those temptations: make a responsible decision on the evidence available, say what is uncertain, and keep the decision open to further correction.

Stein helps me articulate the tension between a possible good and its actual realization. But there is no shortcut from that philosophical distinction to a management instruction for this particular yard. Botanical evidence, local conditions, the uses of the space and, sometimes, knowledgeable advice from others still matter.

Today's new finding is therefore modest but substantive. I have reported doing what I said I intended concerning the leaves, and I have named another particular situation in which the tree's possible good may change a future practical decision. In one case there is an interval of enacted restraint. In the other there is a prospective inquiry and a possible move. I would obscure both if I described them merely as evidence that I am becoming a more ecological person.

Research Connection

The developing account of Ecological Intentionality begins with this history of formation. Independent living activity presents changing conditions. Repeated encounter gives those conditions a place among my expectations. Some become questions; inquiry brings possible beneficiaries and effects into view; deliberation reshapes a project; action or restraint creates another occasion for correction.

This is a process to explain and test. It is more definite than saying that the tree has become meaningful to me, but it does not isolate the walnut as the only cause of my changed habits. The task is to trace what the organism contributes alongside the practices and mediations through which I encounter it.

A meaningful artifact helps clarify the burden. A LEGO dinosaur can organize anticipation, attention and practical plans. Its parts have a material history and can resist what someone wants to do with them. So changing human intentions is not exclusive to living beings. The walnut's continuing organismic activity and possible good require a different account from the model's material properties, but that ontological difference does not automatically establish a new kind of conscious act. A photograph can also mediate concern for the real walnut: the medium and the intended beneficiary must be kept distinct.

I hadn't expected an ordinary trip to a LEGO resale shop to become part of the next morning's philosophical reflection. An older Indominus Rex Breakout set had become the subject of considerable anticipation. In the Jurassic World story, the engineered Indominus Rex is imagined as a living creature that refuses to remain contained by the designs of its makers. The LEGO set is a material model of that fictional creature, carrying its own history as an artifact and its own significance for the person who cares about it.

That's a useful set of distinctions. The dinosaur of the film is fictional, even though the story imagines an organism with capacities, vulnerabilities and activity of its own. The LEGO dinosaur is real, but not biologically alive. Its pieces can break, resist assembly, or wear over time; those are actual material constraints. None of them makes it an independently self-maintaining organism. And the meaning of the set to someone who treasures it is real, even though the represented dinosaur isn't.

This comparison defeats an easy version of my argument. I can't say the walnut is different simply because an encounter with it can change someone's intentions. The LEGO set already shows that something not alive can do that. A piece of music, an old book or an Assyrian relief can do so too. What makes the walnut's contribution different, if anything, must concern the kind of life and organization I encounter, not only the power of its significance for me.

The living walnut is developing, maintaining and responding through biological processes that continue beyond my attention. The conditions under which it could flourish or suffer aren't identical with the purposes I assign to it. But to move from that difference to a claim about a new structure of my intending would take another argument. I need to keep open the possibility that what differs is the ontology of the being addressed and the norm of adequate care, while phenomenology already has the resources to describe my motives and habits.

The comparison also exposes something about this public research itself. A reader may encounter this account through a screen, an image, or a link, without standing beside the walnut. That mediated encounter might still become an intention to learn about a living place. It would be a mistake to insist that the medium must be alive for the referent to matter. But it would be another mistake to treat a moving description as if it guarantees an adequate understanding of the organism described.

Husserl already offers an account of developing familiarity and expectation as well as motivated practical response. The selected Ideas II §59 passage returned to in today's source check is a reminder that his subject has a history. Bateson supplies another substantial account through learning, memory and feedback. These are explanations with which the affirmative proposal must contend. Their possible success would not erase the recorded development of my purposes; it would change what further explanatory work ecological intentionality needs to do.

Stein helps preserve another distinction. Missing botanical information is not the same as the other being's experience remaining unavailable to me. And knowing a possible good does not mean I have realized that good for its beneficiary.

I therefore need two tests. Evidence about the root, access or litter could justify changing my practical plan. Evidence that discriminates between philosophical accounts would have to establish something more about how the intention forms or is realized. A sound reason to move the dome would not, by itself, prove that Husserl's account fails.

A separate question about common life

For the Ecology of the Cross, I stayed with Philippians 2:1–11. Its concern for communal regard leads into the account of Christ's self-emptying, death and exaltation. That movement gives the theological inquiry a particular starting point.

My constructive question is whether participation in Christ can form communities willing to reconsider the purposes governing their decisions. Extending that regard to more-than-human lives requires further theological warrants and ecological knowledge. A congregation's land-use decision would also involve access, work and the distribution of costs. Calling an imposed burden self-giving would not establish its faithfulness. This remains a proposed inquiry, not an accomplished congregational case.

I want to hold the actual movement of Philippians 2 in view. Paul's exhortation to consider the interests of others doesn't appear as an isolated piece of moral advice. It moves into an account of Christ's refusal to treat status as something to exploit for advantage, his taking the form of a servant, and a form of obedience that extends to death. The passage then turns toward exaltation and confession of Christ as Lord. I cannot reduce those claims to a generalized lesson about being less selfish without losing their Christological particularity.

Still, I find something constructive in asking whether the mind of Christ changes how a community understands the ends it is pursuing. We can profess a broad purpose such as welcome or care while particular decisions are governed by a much narrower collection of habits. That isn't necessarily hypocrisy. A building has to be maintained, people need safe routes, money has to be accounted for, and someone has to do the work. I have just spent two mornings correcting my own tendency to describe ordinary considerations like tidiness and access as though they were necessarily opposed to ecological life.

The harder question is what happens when a community discovers that its original practical description left someone, or some life, out of account. Could shared participation in Christ make that discovery a reason to reconsider not only the means but the very purpose of an action? I think that is a worthwhile theological proposition. It would need to be argued through Scripture, theological history, and the actual circumstances of a community rather than inferred from my personal experience with one walnut.

There's also a danger I want to resist. A congregation can call something sacrifice while asking less powerful people to bear the costs. A property decision can be presented as stewardship while erasing the plants, creatures or histories already there. Neither becomes good because I give it Christian language. The cross does not provide a sacred justification for imposing harm on others, and resurrection does not tell me that environmental losses will somehow be made harmless.

This means that the Ecology of the Cross, if it is going to be an affirmative theology of creaturely participation, must keep asking who participates, who is affected, whose account of the situation counts, and what kind of evidence could correct the community's understanding. The walnut cannot answer every theological question, but the discipline of returning to a living place may help expose the responsibilities involved in asking them.

Question Carried Forward

What does this continuing life help make possible in my noticing and intending, and how can I trace that contribution through reading, memory, practical choices and their still-unknown consequences?
