item.description: A blue-sky morning among walnut leaves, ivy and violets complicates what care is for and presses the living-tree comparison against Husserl.
item.content:encoded:
Saturday, November 7, 2026 · Black walnut, Spartanburg, South Carolina · approximately 54 minutes recorded

Prompt

When I say I want to care for this place, whose good is actually determining what I am trying to do?

The prepared question this morning concerned the black walnut and its neighbors, especially the plants growing at the base of the trunk. After yesterday's reflection about fallen leaves and a change in my weekend plans, I wanted to know whether care becomes more demanding when I can name some of the other lives in the picture. I also wanted to push harder on the question from my first comprehensive examination: does the living walnut change my intentions in a way Husserl's account cannot adequately explain?

That second question has been following me for months. It wasn't answered in the prepared script, and I didn't want to arrive with the answer already decided. But I wasn't pretending to be neutral, either. I increasingly think the fact that this is a living tree, rather than an impressively made copy of one, matters to the development of my conscious purposes. Today I tried to say why, even if my reasons still need a stronger philosophical defense.

First noticing: the sky, the leaves and an ordinary Saturday

It's sunny this morning, mostly blue skies after several damp days. The air still has that chilly, wet-leaf feeling of November. I'm out here while the children are home for the weekend, looking at the walnut and thinking not just about philosophy but about what actually needs to happen in the yard.

I've been coming back to the same general view for weeks. Now the upper branches are remarkably exposed, with yellow leaves clinging lower down. The fallen walnut leaves make a broad carpet, but it isn't the bright uniform yellow I remember from yesterday. Some leaves are dark brown, almost black in patches, while newly fallen yellow leaves rest on top. I can describe those visible differences. What happened to each leaf overnight is another question.

On the way over I passed the red maple, whose leaves are covering another part of the yard, and one of the oaks, where acorns have accumulated thickly enough to make walking treacherous in spots. An old oak on another side of the yard has its own combination of leaves and acorns. One backyard, several different kinds of ground cover, several practical problems and possibilities.

A light breeze passes through and I see leaves coming down. Those falling leaves are happening now. The histories of the hundreds already lying beneath the tree are not. The photographs I've been making since September let me compare appearances, but they can't supply all the intervals between them. They also remind me that what I perceive now is full of memory, habit and expectation. That is not a flaw in perception. It's one of the reasons Husserl keeps finding his way into these mornings.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

The walnut on November 7, with the blue sky showing through its upper branches and yellow foliage remaining below. My earlier photographs help me compare the season, but they don't record what I didn't see between visits.

I'm increasingly aware that the tree's changing appearance isn't identical with my knowledge of the living processes producing it. Yellow, brown, bare branches and falling leaves appear to me. Biological development requires another kind of explanation, and the walnut's possible experience, if there is any, is not something I can read straight off those colors.

Looking down: ivy, violets and lilyturf

Today I deliberately turned my attention from the upper canopy to the base of the trunk.

Yesterday I used PictureThis to begin identifying plants in this part of the yard. The app suggested English ivy (Hedera helix), common blue violet (Viola sororia) and lilyturf (Liriope). I didn't stop there. I spent time comparing photographs and sketches with plant books, field guides and other resources. That has made me more confident in the general identifications. Still, I need to write down the diagnostic characters and the exact sources that support them, and I haven't settled whether every clump of lilyturf is L. muscari rather than a look-alike.

That distinction sounds fussy until I consider what I'm trying to infer from these plants. Naming them helps me ask better questions. It doesn't tell me whether they're flourishing, what they're doing to the walnut, or how they affect insects, fungi and the other groundcover.

I can see ivy climbing the bark, perhaps about a foot up the trunk now. There are narrow, grass-like clumps and broader violet-like leaves among the fallen leaf litter. On another side of the walnut the violets appear more prominent. The arrangement is not uniform.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

At the walnut's base. A vine climbs the trunk among violet-like leaves, lilyturf-like foliage, and layers of fallen walnut leaves. The photograph supports the observation of placement and attachment, not a diagnosis of benefit or damage.

Why are the plants distributed like that? I've wondered about light, moisture, the different sides of the trunk, and the history of how this yard was maintained. Those are hypotheses. I haven't measured the light or soil and shouldn't announce a cause on the basis of a photograph.

I also looked toward the two oaks. I recognized more violet-like plants around them, and a great deal of lilyturf near a stone ring around one oak. That isn't a matched sampling protocol. I don't have fixed plots, species counts, moisture readings or a reliable record of every planting decision in these places. But it does move the inquiry forward from “some plants near the walnut” to observations that can be revisited and tested.

There's something delightful about finally naming some of the neighbors of a tree I've spent so many hours thinking about. The names don't reveal their inner lives, but they do make my next ignorance more particular.

One community doesn't mean one harmonious good

English ivy is a living plant. Its growth is not a moral failure because it happens to be a species introduced to this region. Nor does the fact that the violet is native give me immediate knowledge of its well-being or tell me what every management decision should be.

But it's also not true that every living thing in this yard has an equal claim to spread without limits. Clemson Extension identifies English ivy as invasive in South Carolina and explains how established growth can shade or smother other vegetation. That is general ecological guidance. It doesn't prove that this particular vine, visible for about a foot on the walnut's bark, has injured the tree. I want to know what's actually happening before I decide how to manage it.

This distinction reminded me of the bamboo along an adjoining property. I've had to work to keep its shoots from extending into parts of our yard. I sometimes jokingly think of that work as a negotiation rather than a battle, because I don't hate bamboo or deny that it's a living thing. But its vigor can create a very different situation for the plants and people around it. The same general lesson comes up with kudzu, another introduced plant familiar to anyone who has spent time looking at the landscapes of the Upstate.

It isn't enough to say “introduced, therefore bad,” or “native, therefore good.” Some introduced species are aggressively invasive under particular conditions, and some native species can also grow vigorously where we don't intend them. I was reminded during the source review that poison ivy and Virginia creeper are native to eastern North America. My personal annoyance with poison ivy doesn't change its biogeographic history.

The question is more difficult than sorting beings into two moral categories. What is each organism doing? What other lives and practices does its growth affect? Which ecological relationships are supported by evidence? Which ones am I merely imagining?

I love the idea of adding more native goldenrod, partly for pollinators and partly because I want the yard to support more of the relationships that already characterize this part of the Piedmont. But even that good intention requires species and site selection. Goldenrod in the wrong location isn't automatically an act of care, and I won't turn the project into an arbitrary requirement that every plant has to be native to count.

This is where Edith Stein keeps returning. Another being has a life that isn't mine. Its possible good can't be read off my sentiment toward it. And several living beings sharing a space doesn't mean they share the same requirements, much less a single experience.

The purposes of mowing were more complicated than I first said

My decision about the fallen leaves has already changed this week's plans. I'd considered mowing through the walnut leaves again this weekend, and then I read more about leaf litter as overwintering habitat for insects and other invertebrates. I've decided, for now, to leave whole leaves in the naturalized areas rather than shred or collect them.

Yesterday I described that as a change from tidying the yard to caring for the lives supported by the litter. That's part of it. But today I realized that my earlier purposes weren't quite that tidy themselves.

I'd also mowed because I thought it would benefit the soil by breaking down the leaves. And I had reasons involving access, play and moving safely through the yard. Anyone who has walked across a dense patch of acorns knows that it can be slippery. Those are real practical goods, not necessarily expressions of an anti-ecological aesthetic.

So I have to reconstruct the before-and-after more fairly.

I had intended to mulch some of the leaves because I wanted the yard to look orderly, believed smaller pieces would be better for the soil, and wanted useful, safe places for our family. Now I intend to leave more leaves whole because I've learned about possible overwintering habitat and the importance of preserving what lives in the litter.

There is an ecological purpose in both accounts. There are also different beneficiaries, different expectations of what will happen, and possibly a new priority among ends that were already present.

Perhaps the right next action isn't “never move a single leaf.” Perhaps it is to leave substantial habitat where that makes sense, while keeping particular walking routes passable or managing an invasive plant where evidence warrants. I haven't enacted a complete plan for the whole yard yet. This morning doesn't establish that all the organisms here will benefit.

And I need to watch myself here. An intention's sincerity doesn't give me biological evidence of its success. Better information may lead me to choose differently, but knowing a possible good isn't identical with making it happen.

I suspect that point will matter as much to our eventual theological argument as it does to this particular Saturday.

Husserl is still husselin'

Now to the harder part of today's recording.

I've been working since my first comprehensive examination with the challenge that Husserl may already have more than enough resources to describe the phenomenon I call ecological intentionality. It would be too easy to imagine that his phenomenology consists of a detached spectator staring at a passive object, and then announce that a living walnut proves him wrong.

That isn't his account.

The walnut is familiar to me through many experiences and anticipated possibilities. When I see its thinner canopy I see it within a history of earlier canopies, seasonal expectations and habits of returning. My body orients toward the tree, moves around it, and makes different aspects available. Its appearances can attract my interest and motivate investigation.

Within the personal and practical world of the yard, I value the tree, the soil, the family uses of the space and the possibility of other living beings flourishing here. I make plans, revise judgments and reconsider which purpose an act ought to serve. Husserl's Ideas II describes a world that motivates active inquiry and practical response; it doesn't require that I remain in front of the walnut as an unchanging observer.

Roberta De Monticelli's discussion of practical agency, and Michael Barber's presentation of Alfred Schütz, make the challenge even harder. A standing commitment to care can coexist with several immediate projects. Learning may change which reason governs the next action. The very change I care about might already be described within those accounts.

I think that is a strong objection. I also think there is something further to ask.

While looking at the ivy climbing the walnut, I began considering its own continuing growth. It has a biological organization that isn't given to me as one of my personal projects. The walnut's development isn't something I can stop and start with attention. These organisms will have conditions of life even when I leave this yard, and my decisions can meet or miss those conditions.

That's not the same as saying I perceive the ivy's own conscious goals. My description of its growth is partly informed by biological knowledge and partly interpreted through ideas of purpose and flourishing. I can't turn a visible climbing stem into a human-like first-person intention.

And yet I think the actual living organism has made a difference to my consciousness and my practical ends.

I don't mean only that the word “walnut” is a more interesting object of thought than “LEGO tree.” I mean that over these years the tree has grown, changed, surprised me, and made some of my previous plans seem inadequate. I've had to learn what it is, what its leaves and roots are doing, and what might count as care for its ongoing life.

When we first moved here, I even mistook its nuts for pecans. I was thinking from trees I knew growing up. The staining husks, the walnuts themselves, and some investigation eventually corrected that early identification. It wasn't just a prettier way to name a familiar object. Learning what kind of organism I was encountering changed what I could reasonably ask and do in relation to it.

I don't believe I'd have the same practical history with a LEGO tree in the yard. However sophisticated the model, the model itself isn't undergoing the same biological development, vulnerability or seasonal changes.

That's the gap I keep trying to describe. A living being has a history and an independently unfolding good that an artifact as such doesn't have.

But I'm not going to make the inference too quickly. A photograph of the walnut could motivate care for the living tree shown in the photograph. The image doesn't have to photosynthesize for the intended beneficiary to be alive. And a model could lead me to change my plans for real living trees somewhere else. So the comparison can't simply divide “living object makes me care” from “dead object leaves my intentions unchanged.”

Husserl can still describe my learned beliefs, memories, valuations and motivated practical responses to a real organism. The remaining challenge is to say why the organism's ongoing life is part of the constitution of this particular conscious act, and not only its actual object, the cause of my learning, the information motivating the act, or the independent standard by which later care might be judged.

During the recording I argued that the difference survives this Husserlian comparison. I still think there's something missing if we stop with the agent's reasons and representations. But I haven't completed the argument that establishes a novel constitutive structure. I want both things on the record: the positive claim I'm making and the serious possibility that Husserl can account for the example we've given so far.

Stein, Merleau-Ponty, Ruyer and Watts don't give the same answer

There were several philosophical companions in this morning's digressions, and they aren't interchangeable.

Stein helps me preserve the creature whose experience I cannot possess. Her account of vegetal phenomena of life admits a qualified apprehension without granting transparent access to a plant's wakeful “I.” Her account of finite goods also distinguishes what could benefit another being from an event that actually realizes such a good. She doesn't settle the biological condition of this walnut for me.

Merleau-Ponty challenges the fantasy of an isolated consciousness surveying a world from outside it. His later account of flesh describes a shared sensible field, although shared visibility doesn't collapse the differences among individual beings or make their practical goods identical.

Ruyer brings the organization of living form into sharper focus. The claim that an organism maintains a form of immanent activity or self-survey is a substantial metaphysical proposal. It isn't directly photographed when the ivy climbs the bark.

And Vanessa Watts creates a different and perhaps more difficult pressure on the entire exercise. Her account of Place-Thought doesn't begin by treating land as a passive setting for the choices of a perceiving human subject. But she works from particular Haudenosaunee and Anishnaabe histories, thought and political contexts. Her language of land and agency isn't mine to extract as an Indigenous endorsement of a new European phenomenological category.

I need each of these thinkers to be able to disagree with me, and with one another.

Maybe the developing account of ecological intentionality will have to say more about independently living beings, and less about the solitary human perceiver who decides which of them is worth noticing. That would be a substantive challenge to my starting point, not a bit of “relational” language added to a familiar picture.

Beyond the backyard: what is a church actually for?

As often happens in these longer sits, I ended up thinking about Christian community.

In my own church experience, I've seen how easy it is for the purposes a congregation professes and the purposes that organize particular decisions to drift apart. We can talk about mission, love of neighbor and care for God's creation, and then make choices mainly around convenience, budgets, membership, facilities or institutional survival.

That isn't a claim that every congregation behaves this way, or that budgets and buildings don't matter. They absolutely do. But we have to ask whether those things are means serving the community's larger theological purpose or have become purposes that organize everything else.

Imagine examining a new playground, a building project or the management of a church's grounds. Who benefits? What happens to trees, soil, water and the other beings already there? Who is doing the maintenance work? Who gets safe access, and who is left bearing a cost? What would count as evidence that a practice is genuinely caring?

Those aren't abstract questions in our community.

The Good Samaritan in Luke 10 challenges how one becomes a neighbor through mercy, but its immediate subject is a wounded human being. Extending it to more-than-human lives requires a constructive argument. Philippians 2, Colossians 1, Romans 8 and 1 Corinthians 15 offer different Christological, communal, cosmic and resurrection claims, none of which is demonstrated by falling leaves or a more ecologically informed lawn-care decision.

I thought about the Lorax, too. I understand the appeal of someone who says he speaks for the trees. But perhaps the task of a church is not to replace the tree's own life with a human spokesperson. It could be to develop ways of attending, investigating, judging and acting in which the trees and soil are not merely invisible background.

This is a theological possibility I'm trying to construct, not a report of a congregation that has already achieved it. The proposed class on Scripture and ecology remains prospective. I'd want actual communal deliberation, history, appropriate consent and ecological evidence before drawing conclusions about institutional transformation.

And this connects to the walnut in an unexpected way. We can say we're caring for it, but the operative purposes of our next action, or our refusal to act, need to be answerable to the lives affected. I suspect a church faces a version of the same practical difficulty, though its theological warrants and institutional responsibilities add burdens of their own.

What today's sit established, and what it didn't

I left the walnut still convinced that living beings matter differently to our practical purposes than models or objects whose value belongs to human uses alone. I don't think the distinction is merely decorative. This particular tree, along with its changing leaves and the plants growing around it, has reorganized how I notice and what I think I should do.

But I also have better reasons now not to tell an easy story about my own transformation.

The purpose of mowing wasn't only neatness; it included soil and access. The plants at the walnut's base are not one homogeneous community with one interest. My identification work is better than an app guess alone, but it still needs documented diagnostic evidence. I can see where ivy climbs while remaining unable to infer that it has injured the tree. And my recognition of the walnut's living independence is not, by itself, an argument that Husserl failed to describe my act of caring.

Today's positive proposal remains a differentiated answerability of practical purpose to independently living beings. Its philosophical burden is to show whether the other's ongoing life does something constitutive within a particular intention that the strongest existing accounts of motivation, valuation, embodiment and practical action cannot already explain.

If those accounts fully describe this case, I need to say that. If they don't, I need to identify the exact explanatory remainder rather than announce that trees are special.

That's where I think the next stage of the work lies.

Later research note, November 7: formation across encounters

After writing this sit, I clarified a larger affirmative question for the public research roadmap: How does intentional life take shape over time through relationships with independently living beings? This question comes before, though it must still undergo, the comparison with Husserl. Ecological intentionality is not just phenomenology with a greater variety of nonhuman objects. I am asking about the ecological formation of intentional life itself.

Today's ivy encounter is one moment within a longer, uneven history. On October 29 I reported that sustained attention to the walnut had begun affecting what I noticed away from the tree. On November 1 I recorded a particular intervention involving the swing and a spider's web. On November 6 I described a revised plan for fallen leaves, and today I recovered the soil-care and safe-access purposes that were already part of my earlier plan. These records involve reported changes in attention, an enacted action, an intended action and retrospective correction. They are not interchangeable evidence, and they do not prove that the walnut alone caused any change. Reading, memory, practical obligations and other encounters also belong to the history.

The positive phenomenon is that my ways of noticing, anticipating, judging and intending have developed through a sustained relation with a living organism whose seasonal activity does not depend on my attention. Whether this warrants a distinctive constitutive account remains open. Husserl's genetic and practical phenomenology, Bateson's account of ecological learning and Watts's challenge to a human-centered starting point are genuine alternative pressures. The next task is to trace the history carefully: distinguish what the tree did, what I perceived or inferred, what I learned elsewhere, which purpose changed, what I actually did, and what remains unknown about the effects on other beings.

Research Connection and sources

The questions raised here continue through Ecological Intentionality, Husserl, Edith Stein, Merleau-Ponty, Ruyer, Vanessa Watts, Attention, Vegetal Encounter and Place and Agency.

Primary and scholarly anchors under active examination: Husserl, Ideas II §§55–56 (motivation, active response, natural causality), with §59–60 on familiar expectations and ability; Stein, On the Problem of Empathy III.5(i) and Finite and Eternal Being V §§16–17; Merleau-Ponty, The Visible and the Invisible, “The Intertwining—The Chiasm”; Ruyer, Neofinalism chs. 9 and 14; Vanessa Watts, “Indigenous Place-Thought & Agency Amongst Humans and Non-Humans” (2013); De Monticelli and Barber in The Routledge Handbook of Phenomenology of Agency (2021). These do not all have the same evidence status: some passages were previously checked, others remain selected indexed readings rather than completed chapters. See Sources & Reading for the editions and unresolved citation questions.

For botanical questions: Clemson Extension on English ivy, English ivy control, Virginia creeper, and the poison-ivy guide provide regional context. These sources do not establish what is occurring between the particular plants in this yard. The walnut-versus-two-oaks groundcover comparison remains incomplete.

Question Carried Forward

If an independently living being can become decisive among several already valued purposes, what would show that its ongoing life helps constitute my intention, rather than merely providing reasons, new information, an intended beneficiary or the independent measure of whether my care succeeds?

I still want to advance the positive claim. But I want an answer that Husserl, Stein, Ruyer, Watts and the walnut itself could genuinely challenge.

item.title: When Another Life Changes the End
item.description: The squirrels, a falling leaf, and a changed weekend purpose test whether ecological learning alters a plan, its operative end, or the constitution of intention.
item.content:encoded:
Friday, November 6, 2026 · Black walnut, Spartanburg, South Carolina · approximately 39 minutes recorded

Prompt

Can another being's independently unfolding good alter the very end of an intention, rather than only its informational basis, its means, or the norm by which we later judge it?

That was the question I came out with this morning. I didn't expect the walnut to answer it for me. I wanted to find out whether I could name one actual intention, distinguish what had changed in that intention, and let the philosophical account remain open to correction. Last night I had been reading about the fallen leaves and the lives they may shelter. That research had already changed a practical decision I was considering for the weekend. The sit was an opportunity to understand the change more carefully, not a way to pretend the tree caused an action I had already decided on.

Field Notes

The weather surprised me immediately. I'd expected another cloudy morning after rain. Instead, the sun was out, with some clouds still moving through the sky. I came around the red maple, whose leaves are darkening toward red, and noticed the oaks shedding their own leaves and acorns. The walnut stood ahead of me with more and more of its upper branches exposed. The remaining lower canopy looked more yellow than green. Some of that difference comes from remembering yesterday's view, but the open branches and today's yellow are what I can see now.

I've been scrolling back through photographs of this tree from the last several months. They're extraordinary to look through in sequence, not because each photograph holds a complete life but because each gives one appearance through which I recognize the same developing tree. A particular picture shows the light, leaves, angle, and moment in which it was taken. It doesn't show the intervals I missed. The progression encourages me to think about the walnut's living continuity and about the history of my own attention, but I don't want to mistake either of those for a complete record of the other.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

The walnut on November 6, its higher branches more exposed and yellow leaves gathering below. This wider view gives the setting, not the particular falling leaf I watched.

Then the squirrels arrived.

Four or five of them were moving near the walnut when I came out. They ran into the tree and began crossing its higher branches. As they moved, leaves came down. I followed one leaf as it detached and fell and managed to catch it in a photograph. That felt like one of those wonderful, accidental gifts of a morning outdoors. I could point to a particular falling leaf and say I watched part of its course. Most of the yellow sea lying underneath the walnut is different. I can see its arrangement, but not the individual histories of the leaves that now make it up.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

One leaf in descent, November 6. I watched it fall while the squirrels crossed the branches. This photograph holds one instant of its movement. That's different from the larger yellow ground beneath the walnut, whose individual histories I didn't witness.

The bark was still wet and dark, almost black in places, and sunlight sharpened the contrast between the trunk and the remaining yellow foliage. I could hear wrens, and I'd seen Carolina wrens in the yard. Off to one side, the oaks kept announcing themselves with falling leaves and acorns. During a later theological reflection, an acorn actually struck my shoulder. It wasn't especially gentle. The oak apparently wished to contribute a footnote.

The squirrels looked comically busy, but their enjoyment, intentions, and purposes are not mine to read straight off their motion. I watched where they went and what happened around them. Their lived experiences remain unavailable to me. The same limit applies more sharply to the walnut. The tree's branches are clearly part of what makes the squirrels' movements possible; that doesn't mean I can infer a shared intention or the tree's inner life.

Later in the sit I looked down again and noticed fresher yellow leaves resting above older brown material. I didn't rake, lift, or dig through them. The visible layering is worth describing. It is not a direct observation of the soil processes, eggs, larvae, fungi, or other organisms that may be present within it. Those questions take us into another mode of inquiry.

The weekend action I was going to take

Here's the thing that made today particularly constructive for me.

Last weekend I ran the mower through fallen leaves with the mulching setting on. It worked as a way of tidying the yard. I had considered repeating that work this coming weekend, once the rain cleared. But over the last couple of evenings I'd been reading about leaf litter, overwintering insects, and the complicated history of claims about juglone from black walnut trees. What I found changed the weekend plan. I now intend to leave the fallen leaves whole in the naturalized area beneath the walnut instead of mowing them into small pieces or collecting them.

That's not a conclusion I reached by watching the squirrels today. The decision came out of the reading before I began recording. Clemson Extension and the Xerces Society offer good reasons to retain whole fallen leaves as habitat for invertebrates through winter, and to consider what those lives mean for the larger food web. Leaves participate in decomposition and soil processes. But I still don't know the actual species inhabiting this patch of my yard or what any particular individual will gain from the decision. I have a reasonable ecological rationale for a practice, not a local experiment completed with measurable results.

The juglone question is another good example of why the research matters. The older advice about growing beneath black walnuts often makes the chemical sound like an absolute prohibition. Some recent Extension guidance cautions that the evidence for widespread walnut-induced landscape damage is much less straightforward, especially where shade, moisture, competition, and site history could explain poor growth. Other Extension advice remains cautious around genuinely susceptible plants. I can't decide a particular groundcover plant is resistant merely because it is standing beneath the walnut this morning. I'd need to identify it, examine its condition, and make a fair comparison.

So I am not proposing a universal “never touch leaves” rule. In a naturalized area, whole leaves are valuable habitat. In a path, on a dense turf area, or where a particular plant is being smothered, there may be other needs. The question is whose good is served, and what evidence would allow a practice to be corrected. The planned comparison of groundcover beneath the walnut and two neighboring oaks still has to happen. Today I only saw the layers in one place.

A decision can be ecological without being infallible. It can be justified by credible evidence while remaining open to better local knowledge.

Did my purpose change, or just my method?

This is where the philosophical question becomes much harder than it first sounds.

I already cared about the ecological life of this yard. Earlier in October I was talking about leaves as shelter for soil organisms, insects, birds, and other animals. It would be false to say that I woke up yesterday suddenly discovering the value of creatures I had never considered before. I also need to acknowledge that the repeated sits, the readings, and the broader concerns of my life have all contributed to how I think about this place. I cannot isolate one cause and make it responsible for every subsequent choice.

But something important might still have changed.

An overarching commitment isn't necessarily the purpose that governs each particular act. I might care about ecological life and still intend to mow a patch this weekend because I want it to look tidier. I can then learn something that makes other lives more salient and decide that the operative purpose of the weekend should be preserving habitat rather than producing a tidier appearance. That would be a change in what this proposed act, or purposeful restraint, is for. It wouldn't require inventing an entirely new ultimate commitment.

There is a serious rival description, though. Perhaps ecological care was governing the earlier intention all along, and the research showed that I had chosen a poor means. If that is the case, the end stayed constant while the intended technique changed. The outward reversal alone cannot settle which description is right.

I tried to separate four possibilities during the recording. I might gain information about the situation while keeping the same end. I might revise the means or the timing by which I pursue that end. The future condition of another organism might later reveal that my effort failed to benefit it. Or a newly decisive beneficiary might actually alter the immediate purpose governing my choice.

Those four possibilities aren't interchangeable. The third is especially important. My intention to do something good doesn't make the result good for those affected. Edith Stein's distinction between knowledge of a possible good and the events that realize it keeps that difference sharp.

At the end of the recording I say that I think what I'm trying to accomplish has changed, precisely because the decision to leave the leaves is now for the sake of the lives their cover may sustain. I want to preserve that first-person description, not explain it away before asking the question. But it remains a retrospective judgment about my earlier purpose. A stronger record would state the governing reason before a proposed action, then document the reasons, revisions, and eventual results.

That might sound almost comically careful for a weekend mowing decision. Yet it's the sort of ordinary action in which our larger philosophical claims ought to be able to survive scrutiny.

Why Husserl doesn't let me off easily

My first comprehensive examination brought a valuable objection from Jack Bagby: what, exactly, does ecological intentionality explain beyond Husserl's layered account of intentionality?

I keep returning to that objection because it's right to demand an answer.

Husserl doesn't merely describe a motionless consciousness looking at objects. In Ideas II, experience, habitual familiarity, valuation, motivation, bodily action, and personal practical interests belong within intentional life. The world as experienced can draw my attention and motivate reconsideration, inquiry, and deliberate action. I can learn that an earlier expectation was wrong and redirect what I do.

A change of immediate purpose could fit that account very well. So the fact that ecological learning helped me revise Saturday's plan is not, by itself, a proof that I have discovered a different constitutive structure of consciousness.

Stein also raises the stakes for my argument. Her analysis of the phenomena of life makes room for qualified apprehension of plants without claiming access to an awake plant “I.” Her later account of finite goods asks me to distinguish what is good for another being from my knowledge and realization of that good. I want to preserve her discipline of difference, especially when it complicates a theory I am becoming attached to.

There's a meaningful countercase here, too. Last night the children were at LEGO time at the library. A handmade LEGO structure can matter deeply because of what a child was trying to do. An adult may change a plan in order to protect it, although plastic pieces have no organismic flourishing of their own. The meaning of the act can depend on human relationships and intentions rather than an object's biology. So changed purpose and genuine concern aren't exclusive to nonhuman life.

What the walnut adds, if something more is warranted, is a being whose continuing organization and development are not for me or dependent on what I happen to care about. It grows, sheds leaves, and responds to its conditions whether or not I observe it. Other living beings use this place without becoming participants in my personal purposes. Their independent activity and possible goods can correct my beliefs and my actions.

What remains to show is whether that independence helps constitute my particular conscious act or instead supplies the objects, information, motives, and later standards that Husserl and existing accounts of agency can already describe.

I'm increasingly convinced that there's something here worth constructing. Conviction isn't the same as having discharged the philosophical burden.

A more difficult theological question

The Good Samaritan came back into the reflection. In Luke 10, the lawyer begins by asking who his neighbor is; by the end, Jesus asks which person became a neighbor through mercy toward the wounded man. That is a challenge to the way a question about obligation becomes a form of life.

I have been wondering whether something comparable could happen within Christian communities. A congregation might profess love of neighbor, or even care for God's creation, while very different purposes actually govern its budgets, land, buildings, and decisions. To change an operative purpose might be more consequential than finding a better tool for an existing program.

I know from my own religious upbringing how easily the natural world can become the background of a story told almost entirely in terms of human salvation. But that isn't the only Christian tradition, and I can't turn my experience into a history of every church or every theological reading of creation. The Hebrew Scriptures and New Testament, the history of Christian ecological thought, and the social and political conditions of any particular community deserve their own investigation.

The Ecology of the Cross needs more than an analogy about leaves. Philippians 2, Colossians 1, Romans 8, and 1 Corinthians 15 make distinct claims that must be read in their own contexts. A falling leaf isn't the death and resurrection of Christ. An ecological decision isn't automatically kenosis. And neither injury nor vulnerability should be justified by calling it redemptive.

The constructive possibility I want to examine is whether participation in Christ can transform what a community's purposes are actually for, including which human and more-than-human lives those purposes allow to question them. A possible class on Scripture and ecology might someday be a setting for that inquiry. It isn't an enacted or evaluated congregational practice yet.

This theological question and the philosophical question belong in conversation. They still owe their answers to different sorts of evidence and argument.

After the recording: what the sources add

The subsequent source check makes today's claim harder, in a useful way. Roberta De Monticelli's chapter on rational agency discusses plans, commitments, policies, values, and competing reasons. Michael Barber's account of Alfred Schütz distinguishes a projected act from the various forms of doing and imagining that surround it. Both suggest that an existing phenomenology of practical life can already make sense of a broad commitment alongside a different purpose governing a particular action. I need to read their chapters more fully before claiming anything novel here.

There is even a historical caution about telling a story in which Husserl omitted everything that Stein supplied. James Jardine's research into the manuscripts of Ideas II suggests Stein's editorial work may have shaped parts of its discussion of motivation, while Husserl's own manuscripts already contain important accounts of it. The genealogy isn't neatly divided into the separate territories I'd sometimes like to assign to these thinkers.

For now, those are leads and pressure tests from a later source pass, not things I newly discovered by looking at the tree or a claim that the full works have been reread today.

What I'm carrying forward

What began with the leaves and a proposed weekend chore is now a question about the order of practical commitments. I can mean to care for an ecology and still discover that another, more familiar purpose has been governing one of my actions. Ecological inquiry may rearrange that priority. It can also teach me a better means while the purpose stays continuous. And it may reveal that what I called care hasn't served the lives whose good I invoked.

I don't think the walnut has performed metaphysics for me this morning. It certainly didn't control the acorn that hit my shoulder. But the encounter, the earlier photographs, and the biological research have made the next test more particular and less comfortable.

I will have to record what actually happens this weekend rather than treating today's intended restraint as something already done. I'll also need to return to the living plants beneath this tree and the neighboring oaks, ideally with the same observational care I've tried to bring to the walnut itself.

The challenge now is not only to explain why a plan changed. It is to ask whether another being's independently unfolding good has changed what I am trying to accomplish, what might correct that purpose, and which part of that story a philosophy of consciousness still needs to explain.

Research Connection

This sit directly develops Ecological Intentionality, Attention, Husserl, and Edith Stein. The relevant sources are collected in Sources & Reading; this is a dated record of a candidate argument, not a claim of philosophical victory.

Ecological guidance considered: Clemson Extension on November leaf habitat; Xerces Society, *Leave the Leaves!* (2026); Iowa State Extension on walnut mulch and juglone; and Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center's 2010 walnut-understory Q&A. These are not measurements of this particular yard.

Question Carried Forward

What evidence would show that the good of another independently living being changed the immediate end I was pursuing, rather than only the means of pursuing an end I already had? And would that change demand an account beyond Husserl's?

item.title: The Yellow Sea and the Ends of Care
item.description: An open canopy and yellow fallen foliage sharpen the distance between explaining a change and knowing how to care.
item.content:encoded:
November 5, 2026 · Black walnut · approximately 43 minutes recorded

Prompt

What happens when a familiar tree exceeds my expectation? What would move me from explaining the change to knowing how to care?

Field Notes

I come around the red maple by my usual route and turn toward the walnut. I thought I knew what I would see. The openness above and the yellow sea below catch me off guard.

Long upper branches stand against a cloudy sky. Yellow and some green remain lower in the canopy. The bark looks almost black after the rain. Fallen foliage covers much of the ground, where I remember a thinner scattering. That comparison brings earlier mornings into the present view without making them visible again.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

November 5. Exposed upper branches, remaining lower foliage, dark bark, and fallen yellow leaves. The photograph records an arrangement; it does not reconstruct the overnight events that produced it.

During a breeze, I watch some leaves fall from their attachment points. This is a witnessed event, unlike the history of most of the foliage already on the ground. Rain, wind, and seasonal development belong among the explanations to investigate. Their possible involvement does not identify what brought down each piece.

A small long-legged creature on the bark draws my eye. I am unsure of its identification. Later I touch the wet trunk. Water clings to leaves and limbs, bird calls sound through the yard, and passing vehicles interrupt the quiet. My intended discussion of a particular bark feature gives way to the scene before me.

Reflection

Familiarity brought expectations, but the walnut did not have to remain as I expected it. That is a modest proposition with consequences for the way I approach care. A purpose formed through earlier encounters must remain open to what another life is doing now.

The litter question becomes more insistent. What does leaving this material do for the walnut and its neighbors? I have not yet completed the plant identifications or the comparison of nearby groundcover. This morning renews an intention to investigate; it does not report a new management practice.

I need to keep two questions apart. What explains the fallen leaves? What should I do for the lives affected by them? Even a convincing explanation of the fall would not determine whether leaving, mulching, or moving litter is appropriate here. That requires knowledge of effects and a clearer account of whose good I intend to serve.

Care can direct inquiry before it directs an intervention. Inquiry, in turn, can require me to reconsider what I meant by care. It might also confirm the existing practice. I should not require a correction in order to call the investigation worthwhile.

When the explanation is not yet the good

A small part of the morning gives this problem a shape I didn't anticipate. Water clings to some of the remaining foliage. A droplet on a leaf takes me back to things I know from teaching physical science: the way water behaves, the balance of forces at a surface, and the importance of water to living processes. But the particular droplet is not an observation of the tree taking it into its tissues. I see water on the outside of a leaf. Transpiration, uptake, and photosynthesis are different kinds of claims, requiring biological knowledge and, in some cases, measurements I haven't taken.

Likewise, I can watch a leaflet detach and move through the air without having seen the course of development that made it ready to fall. I can reasonably think about season, wind, rain, and abscission without knowing the full causal history of that particular leaf.

I am interested in the way the encounter brings these kinds of knowledge together without making them equivalent. What I see calls on what I remember and have learned. Those resources allow me to form questions I couldn't have asked in the same way earlier in the semester. But the relation moves in both directions: a changed scene can also show where my earlier explanation was too easy.

I intended to look more closely at a part of the trunk today. Instead I was drawn to the exposed branches, the growing yellow cover, a small creature on the bark, and the droplets left by the rain. The intention to observe wasn't abandoned, but it became more particular through what I found.

One difficulty is that this happened in a setting I have come to know well. The surprise is partly a consequence of the long practice of returning. The red maple, the turn, the place from which I see the whole walnut: these have become part of what I expect. I can't claim that the tree alone changed my consciousness. My practice, reading, memory, and prior concerns have helped form the expectation that the scene disappointed.

There is a further difference between the two inquiries that now confront me:

What happened to make this ground so yellow?

What would justify changing how I care for this ground and the lives within it?

A better explanation of the fallen foliage won't answer the second question by itself. For that I need to identify the organisms actually present, learn what available actions would do to them, distinguish the walnut's possible good from the possible goods of its neighbors, and explain why I should favor one practical end over another where interests differ. What I call care could be well-intended and still fail those lives. Equally, careful inquiry might confirm that I need not change the existing practice.

This is the positive possibility I want to keep working with: the good of an intended beneficiary can make an inquiry necessary before an intervention is justified. My intention becomes more specific when I ask what would count as evidence of benefit. But I have not shown that the living tree's independent activity constitutes the conscious act of asking. That remains a philosophical task rather than a conclusion drawn from the yellow ground.

Research Connection

The developing proposal of Ecological Intentionality concerns how purposes become particular and revisable through relations with independently living beings. Today's contribution concerns the formation and specification of a purpose: attention shifts, an explanation is sought, and investigation becomes a more definite next act. Whether the tree's living activity constitutes an ongoing conscious act remains a further question.

Charles S. Peirce makes the proposal both richer and harder. In selected passages of “Evolutionary Love” (1893), he describes love as encouraging independence while drawing its creations into harmony. He also follows the development of a philosophical idea into particular practical cases. These are useful demands on a theory of care: permit another's development, and let concrete situations make the idea more determinate.

Yet harmony cannot be my starting conclusion. The walnut, groundcover, and other lives may have different goods. I have not established a conflict here, but an inquiry that excludes conflict in advance would protect my theory from the very lives it claims to serve. This is a question I bring to Peirce's account, not a botanical claim supplied by his essay.

Husserl's account of a meaningful practical world and motivated inquiry remains a strong explanation of the conscious sequence. Surprise can also occur before an artificial scene; a made object can matter through its history. My task is to explain what the independent beneficiary contributes to this particular purpose, without treating surprise alone as evidence of a new structure of consciousness.

The separate Ecology of the Cross proposes that participation in Christ can transform communal purposes toward forms of communion that do not make vulnerable lives expendable. Its theological statement has distinct scriptural tasks. A congregation considering its grounds would need ecological knowledge, institutional history, and the accounts of affected people. Neither the beauty of yellow leaves nor a generous description of its mission could establish what its choices accomplish.

Could a congregation learn to change its purposes?

This morning the question also extends beyond the yard. I have been thinking about what a possible church class on religion and ecology might become in the spring. A congregation could read familiar biblical texts alongside the actual ecological history of the land it occupies, the people affected by its decisions, and the living communities around it. That would be more demanding than adding a sermon about nature or deciding that every tree is a symbol of faith.

I am especially interested in the difference between a congregation changing a method and changing an end. Installing a new landscape feature, altering a purchasing decision, or earning a certification may be worthwhile. But what is the congregation trying to achieve in the first place? Whose accounts help define that purpose? What evidence could show that an action benefited the place and its neighbors? And could learning from affected lives require the community to change what it understands ministry to be for?

The Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.) has an Earth Care Congregations program, with commitments in worship, education, facilities, and outreach. I think those categories offer a real institutional place to begin. Certification would be a documentable achievement, but not a substitute for evidence that people, other organisms, or a particular watershed are better served. A class could help open the inquiry. It could not certify the adequacy of its own answers.

Luke 10:25–37 has become a useful theological challenge here. The legal expert asks Jesus to identify who counts as a neighbor. At the end of the parable, Jesus asks which traveler actually became a neighbor to the injured man. The Samaritan's mercy involves attention, changed travel plans, bodily help, money, and provision for care beyond the immediate encounter. It isn't only a kindly attitude.

The injured person in that story is human. I don't want to claim that Jesus was explicitly teaching an ecology of intentionality, or that the parable itself establishes the walnut as a phenomenal subject. The extension of Christian neighborliness toward other creatures is an interpretive and theological proposal that other Christian ecological thinkers have made before me, including John Hart in Sacramental Commons. It deserves careful argument, not a retrospective claim of novelty.

Still, the parable gives me a serious practical question: Who becomes a neighbor when another life changes what we think our intentions require? A church can call itself a good neighbor. A company or local institution can use the same language. But calling an activity neighborly doesn't establish its beneficiaries, its actual effects, or its justice. Public claims about benefits need documentary, ecological, and community evidence beyond a benevolent description.

This is where the Ecology of the Cross may have a constructive consequence distinct from the walnut practice. The Christological claims about communion, self-giving, the cross, and resurrection need their own scriptural and doctrinal arguments. They should not turn unavoidable suffering into something holy or demand that already vulnerable people absorb another institution's costs. If participation in Christ calls a community into a less possessive form of life, I want to ask how the community learns to recognize whose goods its choices serve, and whether that recognition can alter its purpose.

For now this is a possible future teaching and research setting, not an approved course, an implemented church project, or evidence that a congregation has changed. People and communities would have their own histories and consent to consider. Any later dissertation inquiry would have to be designed with them rather than making them illustrations of a theory.

The connection with the walnut is not that the congregation is one giant organism or that its purposes somehow resemble the tree's biology. The connection is methodological and potentially philosophical: care can become answerable to beings and histories whose realities are not exhausted by our initial intentions. Whether that answerability constitutes an intention or revises an intention already constituted remains the difficulty.

Question Carried Forward

What evidence would justify the next act of care, and what would show that I had revised its purpose rather than only its technique?

item.title: Rain and Unfinished Purposes
item.description: Unexpected drizzle and the plants beneath the walnut turn a familiar practice of care into a more specific intention to investigate.
item.content:encoded:
November 4, 2026 · Black walnut · approximately 44 minutes recorded, including pauses

Prompt

When care calls for better knowledge first, what would fulfill the inquiry? What would show that another life benefited?

Field Notes

The drizzle is unexpected. Earlier sprinkles have become more sustained, and I hear the rain while looking at wet foliage. Leaves are falling. Yesterday I had wondered whether rain would bring more down; seeing rainfall and falling foliage together today doesn't establish why any particular piece detached.

The upper branches are increasingly exposed. Green and yellow remain lower in the canopy, with neighboring trees overlapping the view. Around the trunk, fallen yellow pieces lie among other leaves, acorns, and living groundcover. I recognize familiar forms, including plants I call violets and grasses, without having completed a species inventory.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

November 4. Fallen yellow leaflets, other leaves, green groundcover, and exposed roots at the walnut's base. The photograph records their arrangement, not their ecological effects on one another.

Looking toward the oaks, the plants around their bases appear more varied to me. It is an informal comparison. I haven't counted species, compared equivalent areas, or established why the places differ.

The marks at the former swing attachment points are still visible in the rain. I can return to them with attention, but their appearance does not settle whether removal benefited the walnut.

Reflection

I welcome the rain. That welcome tells me something about my response, while leaving its effects on the different lives here open. A shared condition need not serve every being in the same way.

The groundcover makes the question particular. What is growing beside the walnut? What does the litter do in this place? Are the plants benefiting from the arrangement, tolerating it, or present for reasons I haven't investigated?

I have usually left fallen material beneath the tree because I understood that as care. Today I state a more specific next intention: investigate the litter and the neighboring plants before deciding whether to change the practice. I do not make that management decision during the recording. Nor does stating an intention establish that the research has been done.

This is a small but useful movement. Care can give direction to an inquiry before it gives direction to an intervention. The inquiry must allow the existing practice to prove appropriate as well as mistaken. Otherwise I would be searching for a correction I had decided upon in advance.

Research Connection

In the working essay *Whose Good?*, published on Carolina Ecology on November 4, I advance an affirmative account of Ecological Intentionality: purposes can become more determinate through answerability to independently living beings. This morning tests one practical extension of that claim, rather than presuming it is established. Today's sequence is observation, uncertainty about effects, a more particular question, and a stated commitment to investigate before choosing what to do. The plants' possible goods help specify what needs to be learned.

Edith Stein gives this sequence a distinction that matters. In Finite and Eternal Being, V §16, pp. 313–314 in the 2002 Reinhardt translation, she distinguishes knowing a possible good from the actual events through which that good would be realized for its beneficiary. In §17, pp. 315–317, she distinguishes a being's own goodness from the goods others may contribute to it. She also places those differentiated goods within an eternal order, a metaphysical account that cannot be established from the plants growing together here.

Applied to this inquiry, learning more could fulfill my purpose as a researcher while leaving benefit to the walnut or its neighbors unestablished. The success of knowing and the success of caring need separate evidence. This is my application of Stein's distinction, not a botanical conclusion supplied by her text.

Hal King's account of situated plant empathy already makes inquiry into growing conditions part of practical engagement. These resources help construct the proposal and test its necessity. Ordinary deliberation and informed care might explain the whole sequence. The stronger claim that another organism participates in realizing an ongoing conscious act remains a further question.

The parallel Ecology of the Cross proposes that communion in Christ can transform communal ends when affected lives cease to be treated as expendable means. Its provisional theological statement requires distinct scriptural and institutional warrants. A congregation considering how to use its grounds would need to investigate whose good an activity serves, what it actually achieves, and who bears its costs. Welcoming rain, completing research, or adopting generous mission language cannot settle those questions.

Question Carried Forward

What must I learn before changing this practice? What would count as good for the lives concerned, beyond my satisfaction in understanding them?

item.title: A Purpose Answerable to Life
item.description: Restraint beside yellow leaflets and a comparison with a made object sharpen the question of whose good gives a caring purpose its content.
item.content:encoded:
November 3, 2026 · Black walnut · approximately 36 minutes recorded

Prompt

Whose good makes this purpose the purpose it is, and what could require me to change it?

Field Notes

The sky looks brighter and bluer than yesterday's gray morning. More of the upper branching is exposed, while yellow and green foliage remains lower down. I catch an imprecise description as I speak: the branches themselves aren't thinning. Their leaf cover is.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

November 3. Sunlight through the lower branching, an open upper canopy, and remaining foliage against blue sky. Neighboring trees overlap the view.

At the former swing attachment point, the little indentations remain visible. I notice little apparent change since the preceding days. Their persistence doesn't tell me whether the tree was injured or benefited from the swing's removal.

Yellow, spotted leaflets are within reach. I wonder when they will fall, then catch myself before touching them. I understand this restraint as care, though I do not know whether a gentle touch would harm them.

Trucks and construction noise interrupt the recording. I move toward a quieter part of the yard to continue. Near the end, I am surprised by the lower foliage still being held, including some green leaves. Branch shapes that were less apparent under fuller foliage become newly interesting. Both the view and the questions I bring to it have changed.

Reflection

An action's purpose matters even when its movements stay the same. Taking down a swing for convenience and taking it down for the possible good of a tree could look alike. Yet clearing an obstruction and benefiting a living branch are different achievements. The action might accomplish one without accomplishing the other.

That gives my concern something definite to answer to. Wanting to benefit the walnut does not settle whether I have done so. Its continuing condition can make my account of the action inadequate, even if my intention was sincere.

The question also applies to restraint. Withholding touch may express care while leaving its biological justification uncertain. I return to the fallen foliage and reconsider whether to mow, mulch, or leave it. The recording contains that reconsideration, not a new practice already carried out or evidence that one option benefits every life involved.

A hypothetical artificial tree sharpens the comparison. A known made object could still deserve preservation as a work, through regard for its maker, or because of a shared history. Learning that it is artificial need not end care. What changes is the account of what that care serves. Preserving a work does not require attributing it the biological good of a living walnut.

Research Connection

The positive account I am developing through Ecological Intentionality concerns purposes becoming specific through encounters with independently living beings. A possible good becomes relevant to deliberation; an action or restraint is undertaken under that description; further knowledge can change the belief, means, timing, or end. The other being need not share the intention for its condition to matter.

Today's refinement is to name the intended beneficiary and what would count as adequate care. That helps distinguish the content of a purpose from the movements that enact it and from its actual consequences. It also keeps the question of how a concern develops over time separate from the stronger claim that another organism realizes a particular conscious act.

Husserl supplies a substantial existing explanation. In Ideas II §50, his personal surrounding world includes value, use, products, and works that motivate further activity. A known artifact's significance therefore presents no obvious gap in his account. Edith Stein's gardener and Hal King's practical plant empathy likewise already connect apprehending a plant with inquiry and action.

The next comparison must give these accounts their full force. If I preserve a replica for its cultural significance and care for a tree's living condition, I have identified different purposes; I haven't thereby demonstrated different structures of consciousness. The further task is to explain how several lives help specify a purpose, and whether that explanation adds anything beyond existing accounts of valuation, deliberation, and learning.

The Ecology of the Cross asks a distinct theological question: can participation in Christ transform what a community pursues? Its provisional statement begins with separate scriptural warrants concerning self-giving, reconciliation, creation's hope, and resurrection. A concrete land-use decision would need its own history, stated purposes, affected lives, and evidence of consequences. A community's own reasons must be heard before assigning theological meaning to its actions, and no account of self-giving should make vulnerable others expendable.

Question Carried Forward

When I call an action care, whose good am I trying to serve—and what discovery would make me revise the purpose itself?

item.title: What Care Becomes
item.description: A thinning canopy and the return to a familiar branch open a question about how care becomes a purpose specific enough to guide action and remain open to correction.
item.content:encoded:
November 2, 2026 · Black walnut · approximately 42 minutes recorded

Prompt

How does care become specific enough to guide an action, and what could change my understanding of it afterward?

Field Notes

The upper branches are increasingly exposed. Yellow foliage remains lower in the canopy, and fallen pieces lie among the green plants around the trunk. Looking from the roots toward the branches, I notice different qualities in the bark. The light may contribute to that difference.

A leaf within reach looks yellow and spotted. I expect it to fall, remembering others that have fallen. That expectation belongs to the encounter, but it is not the same as watching this leaf detach.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

November 2. Exposed upper branching and remaining yellow and green foliage against a gray sky; neighboring canopies overlap the view.

At the places where the swing's straps used to hang, smoother indentations remain visible. I associate them with the straps because of their location and what I remember. Their appearance does not tell me whether the tree was harmed or whether removing the swing helped.

A saw sounds in the background. Birds call, and a squirrel draws my attention toward acorns. Near the end, the sky brightens. Looking up from the same place, I can see more through the canopy. I cannot attribute that changed view entirely to leaf loss; the illumination has changed too.

Reflection

Care begins to acquire content when it becomes a question about this life and this situation. Wanting to care for a tree doesn't yet tell me whether to intervene, leave something alone, wait, or seek better knowledge.

The earlier swing sequence makes that practical. Concern for the walnut made removal worth considering. A spider's web on a strap gave me reason to delay. Later, when the web was no longer apparent, I removed the swing. Returning to the branch opens another inquiry into what that action meant for the tree. These are decisions across encounters, made with incomplete knowledge of several lives.

Today I also question an ordinary practice: leaving fallen foliage near the walnut. I have understood that as care. What knowledge would support or revise that understanding? A familiar practice needs to remain as answerable as a new intervention.

Even the biological inquiry may concern more than one life. Black walnut litter contributes to soil processes, but its chemistry may matter differently to plants sharing the ground. Iowa State Extension and Penn State Extension offer differently cautious guidance about walnut-derived mulch and juglone-sensitive neighbors. I haven't identified all the plants here or tested the consequences of my practice, so I can't infer that leaving or clearing the litter is the right response. The point is to let relevant knowledge help determine what care requires.

Research Connection

The positive proposal I am developing through Ecological Intentionality concerns how practical purposes become determinate through relations with independently living beings. Its sequence is: an adopted purpose, apprehension of other lives, specification of what to pursue, action or deliberate waiting, and continued correction. Another being need not share my intention for its condition to matter to that sequence.

Edith Stein helps develop and challenge this account. In On the Problem of Empathy, III.5(i), her gardener apprehends the condition of plants, investigates causes, and seeks ways to influence them. Hal King develops this practical dimension in “Propagating Plant Empathy with Edith Stein”, drawing on gardening, propagation, water, soil, and sunlight. His interpretation is a constructive resource as well as a serious challenge to any claim that plant empathy stops at recognition. The comparison therefore begins with an account that already reaches into action. Moving from recognition to care cannot by itself establish my proposal's originality.

The further question is how concerns for several lives specify a purpose and its timing. Perhaps one continuing commitment to care explains the changes through new beliefs about what to do. Perhaps the end itself becomes more specific or is replaced. I need to distinguish those possibilities. This account of a purpose developing over time also leaves open the stronger question of what realizes a particular conscious act.

The parallel Ecology of the Cross proposes that participation in Christ's reconciling life can transform communal purposes. Its provisional theological statement gives distinct scriptural starting points for that claim. A congregation's grounds offer a concrete question: what evidence about affected lives could change the purpose of a project? That requires ecological inquiry, historical knowledge, and accountable deliberation. The branch does not establish the theology, and self-giving must never become a demand that vulnerable others bear the costs of an unchanged institutional aim.

Question Carried Forward

What would show that another life changed the end I pursue, rather than its means or timing—and what evidence could make me revise what I call care?

item.title: After the Swing
item.description: After removing a swing, visible bark marks and a remembered spider's web raise a question about how care changes the purposes and timing of action.
item.content:encoded:
November 1, 2026 · Black walnut · approximately 29 minutes recorded

Prompt

What becomes visible after an action, and how can another living being change what I intend?

Field Notes

The sky is gray, and yellow stands out in the thinning canopy. I took photographs earlier in the morning and returned to record. There are fallen leaves beneath the walnut after yesterday's yard work. I did not witness the overnight falling, but a few leaflets fall while I stand here. More sky appears between the branches than I remember from recent mornings.

Yesterday I removed the swing. Today, looking at the places where I remember its straps hanging, I notice smoother, indented areas of bark. The attachment points are available to look at in a different way now that the straps are gone.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

November 1. Yellow and green foliage, open spaces among the branches, and fallen leaves beneath the tree.

An earlier hesitation also comes back to me. When I considered removing the swing in October, a spider had made a web on one of the straps. I delayed the work because I did not want to disturb it. Later I noticed the web was absent. I do not know what became of the spider, but that changed my judgment about when to act.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

A closer view of branching and bark surfaces after removal. The recording identifies indentations at remembered strap positions; the photograph alone cannot establish their cause or biological significance.

Reflection

The swing had a purpose: play. The branch has a continuing life within the walnut that exceeds that use. Returning to the tree has made that difference increasingly consequential to me.

Concern did not supply one instruction in advance. At one point it gave me a reason to wait for the spider. Later, concern for the walnut supported removal. These were judgments about different lives, made with incomplete knowledge. The missing web did not certify that no spider would be affected, just as removing the swing did not certify that the tree benefited.

The bark marks add something to the encounter after the action. I associate them with the straps because of where they appear and what I remember. I still need to distinguish a visible indentation from an injury to living tissue. The marks cannot retroactively become the evidence on which I made yesterday's decision.

Research Connection

The positive account I am developing through Ecological Intentionality concerns how a purpose takes shape through encounters with beings whose lives are independent of it. An initial use becomes open to reconsideration; another life makes a different action matter; a commitment becomes specific enough to guide action or waiting; subsequent encounters can reopen it.

This sequence makes the proposal concrete. Wanting to care does not yet specify whether to remove something, leave it, or wait. A relationship can help determine those particulars without either participant sharing the other's intention.

Here is the positive structure I want to explain: a family purpose, recognition of other living interests, a delay in response to the spider, a later decision for the walnut, and a renewed need to learn from what the action reveals. Care was not an instruction I possessed in advance. It acquired particular commitments across encounters with different lives, even while my wider wish not to cause harm may have remained the same. I want to distinguish changing the purpose itself from specifying its content and choosing its timing.

Raymond Ruyer gives the branch–swing distinction philosophical weight. In Neofinalism, chapter 5, he describes human organizing activity extending into tools and machines (pp. 36–37), while distinguishing an organ's activity from a tool constructed and inspected from outside (p. 44). His account helps me ask what belongs to a living being's own organization and what belongs to the purposes imposed through its use. It does not tell me whether this attachment harmed this walnut or whether removing it was the best response.

Edith Stein gives me another question about living individuality and what remains unavailable from another life. Her distinct account of non-primordial access doesn't tell me what the walnut or spider experiences, or whether either benefited from my decision. But it makes me wary of identifying their lives with the uses I make of them.

The strongest challenge to my proposal is ordinary practical reasoning: perhaps I retained one general end, avoiding harm, and changed my beliefs about means and timing. That would still be a meaningful response, but it would narrow the claim about revised ends. I need to show which part of the purpose changes. Explaining how concern develops over weeks also differs from showing what realizes a particular conscious act in the moment.

All Saints' Day gives the parallel theological work a particular urgency. In the Ecology of the Cross, I propose that participation in Christ can transform what a community pursues, allowing affected lives to question its established plans. The provisional theological statement develops distinct biblical starting points for that argument. A congregation considering its land use would need to ask whose lives bear the costs and whose evidence could change the plan. The swing supplies no proof of that Christology, and generous intentions do not settle the consequences of communal action.

Question Carried Forward

When another life changes whether and when I act, has it changed my purpose, made that purpose more specific, or changed how I pursue it?
