item.title: Through the Thinning Canopy
item.description: A yellowing canopy, falling foliage, and the morning moon sharpen the difference between what changes in view and what explains a conscious act.
item.content:encoded:
October 31, 2026 · Black walnut · approximately 40 minutes recorded

Prompt

What comes into view as the canopy thins, and what remains beyond what I can see?

Field Notes

The amount of yellow surprises me before I begin recording. Whole sections of the canopy look changed from the tree I remember yesterday. Passing breezes bring more foliage down. I try to photograph one falling piece, and the morning moon appears through openings among the branches.

When I return to record, the moon is still visible. Its apparent position has changed since the earlier photographs. Yellow and green remain overhead, and small pieces continue falling. One lands on my shoulder. Later, I follow another falling piece, noticing its irregular passage through moving air. This isn't only a picture of something falling. It is a brief episode in which my gaze follows a movement I did not begin or control.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

October 31. Green and yellow foliage, open sky between branches, and fallen foliage beneath the walnut. This portrait records the canopy's appearance; the recording supplies the account of falling movement and the moon.

Looking upward, I notice my attention moving from the color of the leaves to how many remain. There seems to be more sky available than a week ago. That comparison includes memory. The sky I see now and the canopy I remember are present to me in different ways.

Reflection

I feel sadness about the prospect of a bare tree while leaves are still attached. The future absence already matters to me, but it has not happened. I cannot read that sadness back into the walnut.

An opening changes what I can see from here. It does not make the moon exist, and it does not reveal everything about the living tree that frames the view. A falling piece has a visible path; the history that made it ready to detach remains largely unavailable. I also have to keep open whether a particular piece is a leaflet or a whole leaf.

This gives attention a concrete task: stay with the differences among what appears, what I remember, and what I expect. Husserl gives me substantial resources for that task through bodily perception, temporal horizons, passive synthesis, and remembered familiarity (Ideas II, §§9, 15–16, 59). I cannot take my sadness about the anticipated bare tree as evidence of a new intentional structure. The tree can remain familiar while changing beyond my preferred picture of it.

Research Connection

My proposal for ecological intentionality is that conscious directedness may develop and be sustained through relations with independently unfolding lives. The stronger question concerns what those lives contribute to realizing a particular act.

Following a falling piece gives that question a manageable scale. Its movement changes the visual information available as I try to keep it in view. But a moving artificial piece might also draw and sustain my gaze. The living origin of this piece and the continuing organization of the walnut matter, yet I have not shown that they are needed to explain this particular act of tracking.

Edith Stein offers a different account of living form developing through received materials (Finite and Eternal Being, IV §4, pp. 247–249). Raymond Ruyer pushes the question of temporally organized form and primary self-survey (Neofinalism, chs. 9 and 14). Neither account is a biological diagnosis of this walnut, and neither makes its possible subjective life perceptually accessible to me. They help me distinguish the organism's own continuing activity from my experience of tracking a detached piece.

Gregory Bateson already makes relations beyond the skin part of his explanation of mental process. In “Form, Substance, and Difference,” the relevant circuit depends on the activity being explained, and memory belongs in that account (Steps to an Ecology of Mind, Jason Aronson reprint, pp. 465–467). Feedback and learned anticipation are substantial explanations I need to test, rather than obstacles to a conclusion already chosen.

The comparison leaves a positive question open: can another being's ongoing activity help sustain an intention without sharing its purpose? An answer has to distinguish immediate looking from the longer formation of concern and from whether an action actually benefits that being. Today's encounter makes those distinctions concrete without settling them.

Question Carried Forward

What does this living walnut contribute to a particular act of attention that a convincing artificial counterpart would leave unexplained?

item.title: What Falls and What Carries Forward
item.description: Falling leaves, a squirrel, and acorns interrupt the sit as the question turns toward what repeated encounters carry into other situations.
item.content:encoded:
October 30, 2026 · Black walnut · approximately 44 minutes recorded

Prompt

What carries forward from these encounters when I leave the tree?

Field Notes

Before recording, I looked toward the walnut and saw yellow leaves falling one after another, more quickly than I had expected. I had been occupied with other things. The movement caught me anyway.

Returning beneath the canopy, I find blue sky and sunlight where yesterday there was muted cloud cover. Green leaves remain among the yellow. Open spaces reveal sky and smaller branches. Leaves continue to fall.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

October 30. Sunlight through a mixed green and yellow canopy; the swing remains attached below. The still image records appearance, while the recording documents movement.

A squirrel appears close by while I am looking upward. For a moment we face each other, then it scurries away. I greet it and imagine what it might make of this human beneath the tree. The imagined answer is mine.

Acorns fall from the surrounding oaks. Their sounds interrupt the reflection, as does the crunch of acorns and leaves underfoot. Later one strikes my shoulder. That interruption is immediate and quite uncomfortable. The walnut is the focus of the sit, but it is not the only thing here capable of changing what I attend to.

Reflection

Sunlight and falling leaves appear together this morning. That does not tell me that sunlight caused this particular burst. In the recording I also struggled to distinguish what I was calling individual leaves from the walnut's compound leaves. Botanical descriptions of black walnut explain that its leaflets can fall separately, so I may have been following individual leaflets rather than whole leaves. Biological knowledge helps correct that description without telling me what triggered each detachment. Nor does recognizing the same walnut through a thinning canopy tell me everything about how its living organization persists.

I keep returning to the distinction between a change in the tree, a movement I perceive, and the significance that movement acquires for me. Calling all three relational leaves their differences unexplained.

There is also the longer change I have been trying to describe: returning here seems to affect how I approach other situations. A familiar habit of asking what I cannot know about another life sometimes becomes relevant beyond the yard. I now have particular responses to examine, rather than only a general feeling of greater attentiveness. But a remembered response and its explanation are different kinds of evidence.

That matters for attention. A falling acorn can interrupt me in an instant. A practiced willingness to reconsider another being's situation develops over time. I should not assume they work in the same way.

Research Connection

Gregory Bateson makes the comparison more demanding. In “Form, Substance, and Difference,” he places mental process in relevant circuits of differences, including pathways beyond the skin, and explicitly includes memory (Steps to an Ecology of Mind, Jason Aronson reprint, pp. 465–467). A later encounter carrying effects of earlier activity is therefore not something his account simply overlooks.

My constructive proposal for ecological intentionality is that relationships with independently unfolding lives may help form what we can notice, intend, and become willing to revise. The stronger claim concerns their role in realizing a particular conscious act. It needs a specific account of that role, not only testimony that a meaningful practice has changed me.

I've also added two sources to the reading record that complicate this work. Simon P. James's “On the Plurality of Nonhuman Worlds” distinguishes biological diversity from cohesive experiential worlds, and it does not decide whether plants are conscious. Andrew Trevor Kirkpatrick's Whitehead and Merleau-Ponty: Toward a Process Phenomenology (2020 doctoral thesis, with a separate 2026 book) offers a processual interpretation of flesh and challenges any easy division between Merleau-Ponty's early and later work. I still need to assess his arguments beyond the abstract and contents.

Learning, prior commitments, embodied habits, and philosophical reading remain serious explanations. The walnut's life is not exhausted by its meaning for me, but recognizing that independence does not settle which explanation succeeds.

Question Carried Forward

How does a sustained relation with another living being carry into a changed response elsewhere—and what would distinguish its contribution from learned habit, motivation, and memory?

Concepts: Attention · Ecological Intentionality

item.title: What the Leaves Change
item.description: Falling leaves interrupt an intended observation and sharpen a question about how repeated encounters change attention.
item.content:encoded:
October 29, 2026 · Black walnut · approximately 37 minutes recorded

Prompt

What changes in my way of seeing when the life I return to keeps changing too?

Field Notes

The walnut stopped me before I intended to sit this morning. Its canopy looked unexpectedly yellow. Later, returning under almost complete cloud cover, I found muted light, a slight breeze, and leaves scattered beneath the tree. The difference from yesterday involves memory as well as what is here now.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

October 29. Green and yellow leaves against a pale sky, with fallen leaves below. The changing light is part of this morning's appearance.

Nearby leaflets carry green, yellow, and small spots. Gaps open onto the cloudy sky and branching structures. I follow individual leaves fluttering downward.

At one point I intend to study a particular cluster. Three leaves fall elsewhere, and my eyes follow them instead. My attention has moved before I have given myself an instruction to move it.

Later I return to the nearby leaves. They are within reach, and I want to touch them. I stop myself because I am unsure whether touching would disturb them. That hesitation tells me something about my concern, though it does not establish that touching would cause harm.

Reflection

The canopy is changing unevenly. Some leaves remain green while others yellow and fall. Following a leaf's movement does not tell me the history of its tissues, and recognizing the walnut through those changes does not give me its whole life.

The interruption and the hesitation are different moments of attention. In one, movement draws my eyes away from the object I meant to examine. In the other, a concern about care leads me to withhold a possible action. Neither is adequately described just by saying that the tree and I are connected.

I also find myself wondering how these returns affect encounters elsewhere. I seem more ready to notice that my purposes are not the only ones present. While driving, I find myself considering the people in other cars, whose obligations and reasons for being on the road I cannot know. I've also noticed a practical change at home: I now leave taller grass and other growth around exposed tree roots rather than mowing right up to the trunks, something I began doing intentionally this summer. My reasons include concern for the trees, but I haven't verified the ecological effects of that choice. These are reports about my experience and practice, not yet an explanation of what changed me. Sustained practice, reading, memory, and prior commitments may all matter.

Research Connection

I spent time last night with Gregory Bateson and “Form, Substance, and Difference” in Steps to an Ecology of Mind. His person–axe–tree example places the relevant mental process in a circuit of differences passing through tree, perception, bodily movement, and the next stroke. He makes the system's boundary depend on what we are trying to explain, and includes relevant memory (Jason Aronson reprint, pp. 465–466).

That makes him a demanding interlocutor for ecological intentionality. An immediate shift of attention, a decision not to touch, and a habit that changes another encounter are different things to explain. A theory of ecological learning already has resources for change that reaches beyond the present scene.

The positive proposal I want to test is that repeated relations with independently unfolding lives help form the possibilities and direction of our intentions. Its stronger version needs to show what the living participant contributes to realizing an act beyond information, learned concern, or the conditions under which care succeeds. Moving images might draw my eyes too; art and literature can change how I encounter the world. Those possibilities deserve a serious comparison.

The leaves have given me a concrete interruption. They have not settled its explanation.

Question Carried Forward

What does the walnut's independently changing life contribute to these intentions that movement, memory, learned attention, and a convincing representation would not explain?

item.title: What the Branch Leaves Open
item.description: A removed branch and an unfamiliar trunk feature bring the purposes and limits of care into view.
item.content:encoded:
October 28, 2026 · Black walnut · approximately 33 minutes recorded

Prompt

What can I know about an act of care after I have already acted?

Field Notes

Before recording, I noticed a large branch hanging in a position I didn't remember from yesterday. The wood looked damaged. I took a photograph, examined it from the ground, and pulled it down. It now lies near the compost pile.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

October 28, before removal. A hanging section and exposed-looking wood among green and yellow leaves. The photograph does not establish when the damage occurred or whether the tissues were alive.

Looking up afterward, I cannot identify exactly where the branch broke from. The canopy is still mostly green. Yellow leaves fall every few minutes, bright in the sun. There is a little wind, and the morning grows warmer.

During a pause, another feature catches my attention: a small protrusion high on the trunk, on a side I look at less often. It is beyond my reach. I can see its shape without knowing what produced it.

Reflection

I came prepared to think about the removed branch. The unfamiliar feature brought me back to the tree that remains. I found myself wondering whether it was ordinary growth, an old injury, or something else—and whether I would have asked in quite this way before spending so much time here.

Familiarity seems to change what I notice and what becomes a question of care. It does not tell me that a feature is new, or that the tree needs an intervention. This is one form of remainder: a feature becomes visible while its history stays open to inquiry.

The branch removal had several possible purposes. I wanted the yard to be safe for the children, I wanted the space to be orderly, and I understood myself as caring for the walnut. Those aims can overlap without meaning the same thing, or serving the same good. I did not see the original break, test the tissues, or establish that removal benefited the tree. I can describe the action more confidently than its adequacy.

Research Connection

Raymond Ruyer helps sharpen the difference between a visible arrangement and a living organization. His Neofinalism treats form as continuing activity and considers how component individualities belong to larger wholes (trans. Alyosha Edlebi, 2016, ch. 14, pp. 143, 147, 150–151). That makes the branch's membership a question about more than where it hangs. His metaphysics cannot diagnose this particular branch from its photograph.

For ecological intentionality, I want to investigate how an intention of care develops through repeated encounters with a life I do not control. The protrusion gives that inquiry an ordinary example: prior concern helps shape what attracts attention next. Yet learning and motivated attention may already explain that change. An artificial hanging limb could also prompt removal, and a mistaken judgment about a living branch could prompt sincere concern.

The inquiry needs to distinguish why I act, whether the action benefits another being, and how the intention itself takes shape. Neither good intentions nor mixed motives settle all three questions.

Question Carried Forward

How does another being's continuing life shape an intention of care—and what evidence would distinguish that contribution from familiarity, belief, and the conditions of successful action?

item.title: More Than One Time
item.description: Changing morning light opens a question about care across lives that unfold at different scales.
item.content:encoded:
October 27, 2026 · Black walnut · approximately 33 minutes recorded

Prompt

Can I attend to differently unfolding lives without pretending to experience another being's time from within?

Field Notes

The forecast said fog. Looking into the branches, I find clear air instead. Leaves and grass are damp, as is the ground around the walnut. Green and yellow remain together in the canopy. Below, fallen leaves lie around roots that emerge briefly before returning underground.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

October 27, 2026. Green and yellow leaves spread above the walnut's trunk; the swing remains beneath the canopy, with the fence and climbing dome nearby.

Close to the ground, small mineral flecks catch my eye. The bark feels firm against my hand. Cars sound in the distance. As the sit continues, the light grows brighter on the walnut and neighboring trees. I feel warmer by the time I finish.

Reflection

The roots bring summer's fuller grass to mind. The leaves recall September and suggest the bare branches I expect in winter. Yet memory and anticipation do not put those seasons before my eyes. What appears now is this damp ground and this changing light.

I've been taking photographs of this tree from much the same place, morning after morning, partly because I'm curious what changes between them. The photographs help, but they cannot show me everything that happened in between. Nor do they let me inhabit the walnut's own life from within. Attention can deepen without turning another creature's history into my possession.

What surprised me as I spoke today was where the question led. I started with the soil around the walnut and wound up thinking about the bacteria living in and on my own body. Those organisms aren't human cells, yet the human body depends on relations with them. That's a comparison drawn from what I know about biology, not something I saw happening beneath the walnut today. Still, it complicates the tidy distinction between an individual living being and a loose collection of parts.

The question of care remains just as ordinary: the swing is still hanging from the tree. What would actually benefit this walnut, rather than merely fit my calendar? I don't yet know. Recognizing that another life has its own history and possible good does not, by itself, explain how that life contributes to the intention I form toward it.

Research Connection

I've been pushing back on Raymond Ruyer while reading Neofinalism. He argues that a living form cannot be understood from a snapshot alone. In chapter 9, he describes an organism in terms of processes that unfold in space and time (trans. Alyosha Edlebi, 2016, p. 100). In chapter 14, he says living beings continue to form themselves rather than operate like finished machines (p. 147). These are philosophical arguments about organizing activity, not things I can confirm by looking at a damp patch of soil.

Ruyer also offers a stronger answer to my objection than I first wanted to give him. His account of organized wholes includes component individualities, sometimes relatively subordinated by the whole (pp. 143, 150–151). But what about relations among the walnut, soil organisms, and other independent lives that don't become its organs? Can there be genuine organization without a single subject surveying it all?

This is a question for my developing account of ecological intentionality, not a finding that settles it. The differing rhythms of our lives may matter to how I sustain an intention of care. But I still need to show what another being's actual activity contributes to that intention beyond shaping my beliefs, correcting my expectations, or determining whether care succeeds.

Question Carried Forward

How could another being's independently unfolding life help sustain an intention of care, beyond changing what I know or what successful care requires?

Concepts: Attention · Ecological Intentionality

item.description: Moving behind the walnut's trunk brings a bodily response into a question about how intentions take shape.
item.content:encoded:
October 26, 2026 · Black walnut · approximately 40 minutes recorded

Prompt

What could this particular tree change about the intention I bring to it, without needing to intend what I intend?

Field Notes

The morning is cool, with blue sky and bright light through the canopy. Squirrels moving around a neighboring oak draw my attention. The swing remains attached to the walnut, with green leaves on a nearby branch that hangs lower. Behind the branches are the fence and power lines.

Close to the trunk, I notice the bark's ridges catching the light. The furrows stay dark. Browns and darker browns become distinct as I look. Grass, fallen leaves and a few small branches lie below.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

October 26, 2026. Morning light catches green and yellow leaves above the walnut's shaded trunk; the swing remains below.

Toward the end of the sit, I notice where I am standing. Behind the trunk, the sun no longer glares into my eyes. I have moved into a place where I can keep looking at the canopy more comfortably, almost without telling myself to move.

Reflection

I came with a question about purposes: how an intention might remain open to another being's life. The movement into shade brings my own body into that question. My position changes with the light, and the changed position alters how I can continue looking.

This is a modest but concrete part of attention. The walnut matters to what I can do here without sharing my purpose. Its life also exceeds the shade it provides for me.

But a screen could block the sun as well. The relief I experience does not, by itself, tell me what difference the tree's being alive makes to the movement. And moving to see comfortably is a different activity from deciding what would benefit the walnut. The unresolved swing question still requires knowledge of the actual tree and attachment.

Research Connection

Maurice Merleau-Ponty gives the movement a strong existing explanation. In Phenomenology of Perception (Part One, chapter 3, on the body's spatiality and motricity), his account of motor intentionality describes bodily directedness that need not begin with a represented plan. The movement into shade is a case to consider through that account. It does not establish a new structure merely because a tree is involved.

Raymond Ruyer sharpens a different distinction. In chapter 14 of Neofinalism, he treats form as continuing formation and considers how individual activities relate within a larger organized whole (trans. Alyosha Edlebi, 2016, pp. 147, 150–151). His metaphysical account makes ongoing activity a demanding starting point for comparison. He also allows that a tightly organized whole may subordinate the individuality of its components (pp. 150–151). Our question is whether relations can contribute to an intention while other lives remain independently organized. Neither his account nor my movement into shade licenses treating the tree and observer as one individual.

The positive proposal of Ecological Intentionality is that our directed activity may take shape through relations with beings that do not share our aims. Its stronger claim—that their independent living activity helps realize an intention—still needs an account that distinguishes it from bodily adjustment, learning and changing plans. Today makes the particular activity under examination easier to name.

Question Carried Forward

What does another being's ongoing life contribute to my intending beyond what a similarly placed screen could make possible—and which intention am I asking about?

item.title: The Branch and the Purpose
item.description: A still-hanging swing brings different histories and purposes into one encounter without making them one intention.
item.content:encoded:
October 25, 2026 · Black walnut · approximately 28½ minutes recorded

Prompt

What does another being's ongoing life contribute to the formation of a purpose it does not share?

Field Notes

Bright light catches the walnut's crown. Yellow and green leaves stand against blue sky; fallen leaves and acorns lie below. The swing is still hanging, its straps and rings visible above the circular seat. Yesterday's intention to take it down has not become a completed act. The children were still playing on it last night while we gathered around the fire pit and made s'mores. When I mentioned taking it down, they weren't quite ready to let it go. Their wishes are part of what I remember this morning, but I can't take them as a measure of the walnut's good.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

October 25, 2026. Morning light through the walnut's branching crown. The neighboring canopy shares the view without disclosing the full relationship between the trees.

Looking up, I notice more yellow than green. Yet I cannot easily separate this morning's appearance from my memory of yesterday. A little later, a gentle breeze moves the smaller branches, and the light has changed again.

Reflection

The swing makes a human purpose easy to recognize. The branch has a different history, belonging to a life that did not develop in order to support that purpose. My concern about the arrangement is a third activity, still unfinished.

These histories meet without becoming interchangeable. Remembered use helps shape what the swing means to me. The tree's condition matters to whether an intervention would help it. Neither consideration tells me that I know the walnut's good simply by looking, or that the tree shares my intention.

The overlapping canopies offer another version of this difficulty. I see leaves and branches occupying the same view. Growth over time, competition, and the condition of each tree require more than that view can provide. Their relation may matter greatly while remaining only partly understood.

Research Connection

Raymond Ruyer gives this comparison a useful complication. In Neofinalism, he describes organic activity extending into manufactured tools and machines, which can be organized by form without being living organs (trans. Alyosha Edlebi, 2016, pp. 36–37). He also distinguishes an organ from a tool constructed and inspected from outside (p. 44). An attachment can belong to an organized practice without becoming part of the tree's living body. Ruyer's further account of living form and the distinction between organized human activity and an organ are philosophical claims, not a diagnosis of this branch.

Husserl's Ideas II (trans. Richard Rojcewicz and André Schuwer, 1989, §§49–51, 55–56) also describes a familiar practical world in which memory, valuation, and motivation can alter what I intend. The changed purpose alone doesn't establish a newly constituted consciousness.

That leaves a question for Ecological Intentionality: how does a purpose develop when it relies on another independently living being? The walnut is more than the meaning I assign to it, but that does not establish that its activity constitutes my conscious intention. It may shape what I learn, what I notice, and what I can successfully do. A stronger account must explain what the ongoing relation contributes to intending itself.

This morning keeps that positive proposal concrete. A purpose formed in relation to another life need not be a purpose shared by that life. Understanding the difference is part of learning what participation could mean.

Question Carried Forward

How could I distinguish another being's contribution to my intending from what I believe about it and what would make my care succeed?

item.title: A Purpose the Tree Does Not Share
item.description: A swing attachment raises a question about how a living tree can matter to an intention it does not share.
item.content:encoded:
October 24, 2026 · Black walnut · approximately 14 minutes recorded

Prompt

How might another being's independent life shape a purpose it does not share?

Field Notes

The morning is cool and sunny. Light passes through green and yellowing leaves, with openings of blue sky between the branches. From farther away, the walnut's crown and the neighboring canopy appear to overlap. Moving closer brings furrowed bark, dotted leaflets, and the junctions of smaller branches into view.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

October 24, 2026. The branching crown in morning light, with the swing below. Overlapping profiles do not establish contact between the trees.

At the swing attachment, I can see a small gap between the loop and the branch. The loop does not look tight at this moment. That view cannot tell me what pressure occurs during use or what the attachment means for the branch over time.

Reflection

The swing has a human purpose. The branch developed within a life that was not organized to provide us with a support. These histories meet in one place without becoming the same history.

I intend to take the swing down for the cooler months. Concern for the tree is part of that intention, although I have not established that removal will benefit it. Care needs to remain answerable to what happens to the being cared for. Confidence in my purpose cannot supply that answer.

Imagine an identical-looking manufactured support. If I knew it was artificial, my concern for its living condition would fall away. Yet that comparison leaves a difficulty: knowing something different can already explain intending something different. An artificial support could still have material organization, a history, and practical value. What it would lack is this walnut's particular living development.

Place and Agency matters here because the tree's possibilities extend beyond the uses we make of it. A shared setting does not imply a shared purpose or a single good.

Research Connection

Husserl's account of practical surroundings, valuation, and motivation in Ideas II gives a strong explanation of how a familiar object can draw attention and prompt reconsideration of a plan. The move toward concern does not by itself require a new kind of intentionality.

Raymond Ruyer complicates the other side of the comparison. Chapter 14 of Neofinalism extends his account of organizing activity beyond biological organisms to microphysical individuals, while distinguishing their capacities (trans. Alyosha Edlebi, Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press, 2016, pp. 142, 147, 149, 151–52). His metaphysical proposal prevents a simple opposition between living form and wholly inert matter; it does not establish the walnut's consciousness or the effects of this attachment. In chapter 13, contingent events can also modify the themes guiding activity (p. 137). A purpose changed by an encounter is therefore a starting point for comparison, not sufficient evidence of a new intentional structure.

The constructive question for Ecological Intentionality is whether another being's ongoing life can help organize our directedness without sharing our intention. The walnut's condition plainly matters to whether attempted care benefits it. Whether its activity also helps constitute the conscious intention requires a further argument. This morning gives that argument a concrete task.

Two wider conversations keep this from being only a debate between European philosophers. In “Indigenous Place-Thought and Agency Amongst Humans and Non Humans” (Decolonization 2, no. 1 [2013]: 20–34, esp. 21), Vanessa Watts questions a separation of place and thought within particular Indigenous cosmologies. Her position isn't interchangeable with the claim that everything causally affects everything else. In “Ecowomanism: An Introduction” (Worldviews 20, no. 1 [2016]: 5–14), Melanie L. Harris foregrounds lived histories and environmental justice. Together they challenge any casual talk about what we intend while leaving land, memory, responsibility, and unequal exposure unexamined. Neither text makes today's swing attachment into evidence of its own philosophical or political claims.

Question Carried Forward

What does the walnut's independent life contribute to my intention beyond what I believe about it—and how could I tell?

item.content:encoded:
October 23, 2026 · Black walnut · approximately 24 minutes recorded

Prompt

What changes about an adequate description when I recognize this walnut as a living being?

Field Notes

Sunlight reaches the green and yellow canopy. The air is cool. Birds and traffic are audible, and leaves and acorns crunch underfoot. One walnut catches my eye on the ground; I cannot see another in the canopy. Squirrels cross the yard.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

October 23, 2026. Morning light through the walnut's canopy, with the swing below. The wider view records the arrangement without explaining the histories of individual branches.

I return to a branch photographed from two positions roughly ten feet apart. From the second position, smaller branches near its abrupt end become easier to distinguish. The light has changed since the photographs were taken. I see more, but cannot identify a belief I have had to withdraw.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

The same branching area from two places roughly ten feet apart. These are different available appearances, not evidence of an overnight biological change or a corrected belief.

Near the swing strap, two smaller branches meet a larger limb. One turns upward; the other droops down. Their different directions hold my attention. I remember both bearing walnuts. That remembered fruiting tells me something about their history, but does not settle their present condition.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

Two differently oriented branches and the human-made swing attachment share one view. The photograph records their visible arrangement, not why the branches developed as they did or what the strap is doing to the tree.

Reflection

The strap and the smaller branches are all visibly attached. Yet I understand their attachments differently: the branches participate in the walnut's growth; the strap belongs to an arrangement of human play. That distinction draws on what I know about trees as well as what I see. The strap is part of an organized human practice, but not a living member of the walnut. The picture cannot explain why these particular branches developed differently or what the strap means for their condition. It recalls an earlier sit, Attachment Is Not Membership, without settling the question of the tree's health.

This is one difficulty of vegetal encounter: familiarity can help me recognize a life while leaving its particular history largely unexamined. Edith Stein's account of differentiated living form gives me another philosophical comparison, but I can't read the tree's individual development or interiority directly from a junction. I have passed these branches many times. Today I pause over their difference without yet knowing how to explain it.

Recognizing a living tree gives my questions a direction. I want to learn what supports or impairs its continuing development. My attachment to the walnut does not supply those answers, or decide which response would count as care. The swing also belongs to the human history of this place, something that Place and Agency keeps in view without turning ecological relation into a single shared good.

Research Connection

Husserl already offers a strong account of bodily changes of perspective and of appearances motivating further inquiry in Ideas II (§§18, 55–56). Today's movement and questions fit within that account. Seeing another aspect does not by itself establish a new kind of intentionality.

Raymond Ruyer asks a stronger question in chapter 9 of Neofinalism (Alyosha Edlebi's 2016 translation). On p. 94, he ties absolute survey to the problems of consciousness and life. Later (pp. 99–101), he treats self-survey as active organization and describes an organism's form through development, not merely an observer's snapshot. His chapter 5 (pp. 36–37) complicates an easy opposition: human-made tools and machines can be organized by form without becoming living organs. So the swing strap isn't simply an unorganized object, but neither is it a growing part of the tree. These passages come from a source check of the English text; the printed-page images still need comparison. None of these claims establishes that this walnut has primary consciousness.

Merleau-Ponty's late account of flesh asks how perceiver and perceived belong to a shared sensible world while remaining different. That question reaches beyond improving my view, but this morning does not decide its explanatory contribution.

For Ecological Intentionality, the test remains whether the term helps explain something these accounts and ecological investigation leave unresolved. Recognizing the need to learn more is a beginning, not yet an answer.

Question Carried Forward

item.description: Abrupt branch ends, a remembered pruning event, and changing light distinguish a known intervention from its uncertain consequences for a living tree.
item.content:encoded:
October 22, 2026 · Black walnut · approximately 26 minutes recorded

Prompt

What can I see where this walnut's growth meets a cut, and what would let me judge the consequences for the tree?

Field Notes

The morning is cool and clear. Green and yellow leaflets interrupt the blue sky. On the side of the walnut near the power lines, several branches end abruptly. I follow one back toward the larger limb, looking at its outline and the leaves nearby.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

October 22, 2026. The whole walnut in the yard, with the fence and neighboring trees in view. This wider photograph locates the encounter but cannot account for the history of individual branches.

One end looks covered over. From where I stand, the surface seems to continue across what I take to be an older cut. I can describe that appearance without knowing what has happened beneath it.

I move a few feet. The illumination of the branches and trunk changes more than I expected. The branching pattern becomes easier to see, and the texture of the bark catches my attention. Looking upward, I see more sky than I remember from earlier visits. The open spaces are present now; the comparison belongs to memory.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

October 22, 2026. Abrupt branch ends beneath the leafy canopy. The photograph records their visible outlines without establishing the history or condition of each end.

From the trunk I can trace three large branches into smaller branches and finally into leaflets. Beyond them are neighboring trees, a fence, and the line corridor. Squirrels move on the ground. Traffic is audible beyond the yard. The light continues to draw me away from the cuts and back toward the canopy.

Reflection

I remember witnessing one pruning event and can identify the branch involved. I also remember asking a member of the power-company crew to be gentle with the walnut. He listened and shook my hand. I came away feeling that the conversation mattered, but I can't establish that it changed what they did. Remembering the event gives me something more than a guess from a branch's present shape. It still doesn't explain every similar-looking end, and it doesn't tell me what the intervention has meant for the tree over time.

This makes the remainder more specific. For one branch, part of the history is available through recollection. For others, the history is uncertain. Even in the remembered case, the biological consequences remain to be investigated. A surface that appears covered over is not enough to decide whether the tree has recovered, remains impaired, or needs any particular intervention.

The power lines also bring different goods into the same view. The walnut's growth and the maintenance of an electrical system meet here. Their proximity doesn't make their interests identical. Place and agency becomes a question about whose decisions shape this encounter, what knowledge those decisions require, and who bears their consequences.

My attachment to the walnut makes me want to care for it. It does not settle what care should involve.

Research Connection

Husserl already gives this encounter considerable philosophical room. In Ideas II, an experienced feature can motivate attention, movement, comparison, scientific investigation, and practical deliberation (§§55–56). His account of communicating persons (§51) also helps describe my request to the pruning crew and their response. That human exchange does not establish that my request changed the pruning, much less that the tree and I participated in the same kind of interpersonal understanding. Remembering a cut, investigating its effects, and reconsidering a judgment need not require a new kind of intentionality.

Merleau-Ponty keeps bodily perspective central. His early account can already help describe why moving changes what is available to me. His late account of flesh poses a further question about the sensible world to which both perceiver and perceived belong. Today's light does not decide what that ontology adds.

Raymond Ruyer now makes another distinction consequential. In chapter 9 of Neofinalism, absolute survey concerns the unity of a form itself. It is not my overview of the canopy, nor an observer hidden inside the tree inspecting its parts. His argument extends to primary consciousness, a stronger metaphysical claim than the visible continuity of trunk and branches establishes. I need to understand that argument before borrowing its conclusion to explain a cut's aftermath.

For Ecological Intentionality, the task is to keep these questions answerable to their different evidence. Whether that discipline contributes anything beyond existing phenomenology, biological inquiry, and environmental ethics remains open.

Question Carried Forward

Once I know that a branch was cut, what further evidence and reasons would justify calling the intervention damaging, beneficial, or an act of care?

item.title: A Shared Morning
item.description: Changing light, a high bark feature, and a squirrel's brief arrival distinguish what draws attention from what explains another being's history or experience.
item.content:encoded:
October 21, 2026 · Black walnut · approximately 17 minutes recorded

Prompt

What does sharing this morning let me encounter, and what will require a different kind of inquiry?

Field Notes

I stand beneath a different part of the walnut, with the sun behind it. High on the trunk, near its division into large branches, a projecting feature catches my eye. It is above my reach. I have noticed it before, but not in this light.

Part of the trunk is lit and part lies in shade. I walk between sunlight and shade, feeling the cold in my own body. Even a small shift of weight changes what I notice on the bark. As the visit continues, I see the light moving across the branches and leaves.

Yesterday I attended to a lower, familiar knot while touching the bark. Today's higher feature remains at a distance. I photograph it without learning how it formed.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

October 21, 2026. A raised, rounded bark feature near the branching trunk. Its visible form does not establish its cause or history.

Near the end of the visit, a squirrel runs along a branch and briefly pauses. I have the impression that we are looking at one another. I try to take a photograph, but it moves away before I manage it. For a moment, my attention follows a different living being through the same tree.

Reflection

There are two questions in my interest in the bark feature. Why did it catch my eye this morning? And how did it come to have this form?

Light, position, and familiarity belong to the first question, though I have not established exactly how they combined to draw my attention. The second asks for evidence about the tree's history. A clearer photograph might help describe the feature. An earlier photograph might show that it was already present. Neither would necessarily explain how it arose.

Paying attention makes the question more definite, but it doesn't supply an answer. The remainder is also more specific now: I can see the feature, I don't know its history, and I have to decide what kind of inquiry could tell me more.

The squirrel brings another distinction. I can report its movement and my impression of being looked at. The humorous commentary I imagine it making belongs to me. Its particular thoughts remain unknown. Sharing this encounter does not make our experiences identical, and the animal's presence tells me nothing directly about the walnut's experience.

Research Connection

Returning to Husserl after the sit, I find that Ideas II already has substantial resources for what happened. An experienced feature can catch my interest, motivate movement or comparison, and send me toward further investigation. Husserl also distinguishes understanding why I became interested from explaining what caused the feature to form. I can't claim a new kind of intentionality merely because looking has led me toward a biological or historical question.

Merleau-Ponty makes the bodily part of the encounter harder to overlook. His earlier work already gives me movement and a situated capacity to perceive. His late account of flesh asks a further ontological question about the sensible world to which my own visible body belongs. I'm still working out what this adds. Neither shifting light nor a squirrel's glance establishes that ontology, much less that the walnut perceives me as I perceive it.

For Ecological Intentionality, I still have to ask what this practice contributes beyond those accounts and existing ecological inquiry. If I learn how the protrusion formed, I may see it differently or reconsider a judgment. But I would need to show how that change happens and why my proposed term explains anything that existing approaches don't.

Question Carried Forward

How might learning this feature's history change the way I see it, and what evidence would warrant that change?

item.title: What Touch Leaves Open
item.description: Touch brings the walnut's bark into closer acquaintance while leaving its history, experience, and needs open to inquiry.
item.content:encoded:
October 20, 2026 · Black walnut · approximately 22 minutes recorded

Prompt

What can touching this walnut disclose, and what will remain to be learned?

Two questions stand behind this morning's encounter: What does late Merleau-Ponty's flesh explain beyond Husserl and early Merleau-Ponty? And what, if anything, does ecological intentionality explain beyond those accounts and careful ecological inquiry? The photograph won't settle either question.

Field Notes

The morning is cold and bright. I feel the cold in my hands and face. Looking up from beside the trunk, I see blue sky through the canopy and sunlight catching the branches. Yellow leaves remain among the green.

I touch a familiar place on the bark with my hand, then with the back of my hand, then my forearm. Roughness, temperature, and pressure become part of the encounter. As my right hand rests against the trunk, my weight shifts toward my right leg.

One knot holds my attention. Its form is plainly there, but I do not know how it came to be this way. Contact has brought the bark closer without explaining its history.

Later, light on the leaves and bark catches my attention again. I begin to call it different, then hesitate. What I can say is that I am noticing something I had not expected to notice. That does not tell me whether the light itself has changed or whether my attention has.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

October 20, 2026. My hand rests against the walnut's textured bark. The photograph documents physical contact, not what the walnut experiences.

Reflection

Touch adds something real. A surface I can see becomes a texture I feel, and attending to it changes how I stand. The gain is specific enough to describe without making it answer every question.

The knot gives Remainder a particular shape. It also keeps the question of Vegetal Encounter concrete: the walnut's living history cannot be read off the texture I feel. It is available to sight while its causal history remains unknown. Further investigation might explain that history. Whether the tree has an experience of this contact is a different question, and my own tactile sensation does not settle it.

Attention includes recognizing these differences. Familiarity can help me notice the bark more closely while leaving the work of understanding the organism unfinished. Even a better understanding of its condition would require further reasons before becoming a judgment about what I ought to do.

Research Connection

Husserl already offers substantial resources for this encounter. In Ideas II, the body is both a material thing and a sensing body; movement, familiarity, and motivated attention help organize what appears. My shift of posture and interest in the knot do not by themselves demand a new kind of intentionality.

Maurice Merleau-Ponty makes flesh a question about the sensible belonging within which perceiver and perceived become differentiated. In The Visible and the Invisible, bodily reversibility remains incomplete, and world-flesh is distinguished from the body's sensing itself. The account distinguishes feeling an external texture, bodily self-sensing, and a hand touching another hand. Today I touched the bark with several parts of my body; I did not clearly perform the hand-touching-hand reversal. That difference matters: bringing different parts of my body against the bark does not establish an exchange of experiential roles between the walnut and me. What the later ontology adds beyond earlier accounts of embodied perception remains a philosophical question.

Edith Stein helps keep apprehension of living condition distinct from causal explanation and possession of another's experience. Her gardener comparison allows cultivated perception to matter without making it an automatic diagnosis. The visible knot asks for that distinction to be taken seriously.

For Ecological Intentionality, the task is still to show what this practice contributes beyond those accounts and existing ecological inquiry. Today's touch supplies a concrete case. It leaves room for learning without promising that closer contact will make every kind of distance disappear.

Question Carried Forward

What would I need to learn about this particular walnut before the intimacy of contact could inform a well-grounded act of care?

item.title: What a Clearer View Leaves Open
item.description: Moving around the walnut clarifies a branch profile while leaving its living processes and the grounds of care open to further inquiry.
item.content:encoded:
October 19, 2026 · Black walnut · approximately 24 minutes recorded

Prompt

What will moving let me see, and which questions will a clearer view leave open?

Field Notes

The morning is cool and bright. Blue sky shows through a canopy still mostly green, with yellow leaves among the foliage. Fallen leaves lie along the ground. I look toward two large branches and the opening between them, a place my attention has returned to many times.

From where I begin, the branches overlap. I expect that moving might separate them in view. Several steps to the left do just that: the two branches become clearly distinguishable. Another part of the trunk comes into view, and I notice yellow leaves I had not noticed from my first position.

The light changes too. I stand more directly in the sunlight, looking at its passage through green and yellow foliage. Getting to this position means stepping over leaves already fallen.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

October 19, 2026. The walnut's branching canopy in autumn light, with the swing below. The portrait records visible foliage and attachments; it does not establish their effects on the tree.

The branches look clearer from here. The tree has not had to surprise me for the movement to be worth making.

Reflection

The separation in view is something I had anticipated. The additional yellow leaves give me more detail. Neither amounts to discovering that a previous belief was false: I had not mistaken the two branches for one. And noticing yellow leaves from a new position does not mean they changed color while I moved.

Attention includes noticing what kind of gain has actually occurred. A fulfilled expectation, an unexpected detail, and a corrected judgment can each matter without becoming interchangeable.

Remainder becomes more specific here. Another surface is now available, while the history of fallen leaves and the processes sustaining these branches remain questions of a different kind. Changing position can answer one question without answering those others.

The attached swing makes the distinction practical. Seeing how something is fastened to a branch does not tell me whether it is harming the tree. An intention to care needs more than a clearer view or a feeling of concern.

Research Connection

Husserl gives this small movement a substantial explanation. His account in Ideas II includes bodily movement, changing appearances, habitual expectation, and attention motivated by what appears. One tree can remain present across partial views without a new kind of intentionality being needed to connect them.

Maurice Merleau-Ponty makes the comparison harder rather than allowing an easy departure from Husserl. His early phenomenology already treats movement as a bodily way of inhabiting the world. In the later The Visible and the Invisible, he explicitly draws on Husserl when discussing how a corrected appearance can be retained within a fuller understanding. Flesh proposes a further account of the relation between perceiver and perceived, but shared sensible belonging does not establish that the walnut experiences this encounter as I do.

Edith Stein helps distinguish the branch's membership in a living organism from the swing's material attachment. Her account of living form also gives a philosophical place to the question of what is good for this particular being. It does not diagnose the attachment's effects or settle what I ought to do. Those steps require further evidence and reasons.

For Ecological Intentionality, two questions remain separate: what the later account of flesh adds to embodied perception, and what this ecological practice adds beyond the accounts already available. Today's movement supplies a concrete case to examine. It does not settle either question.

Question Carried Forward

What further evidence and reasons would turn a clearer view of this walnut into a better-grounded response to its life?

item.title: What Returning Makes Present
item.description: Returning to the walnut brings anticipated autumn changes into view without revealing the history between visits.
item.content:encoded:
October 18, 2026 · Black walnut · approximately 22 minutes recorded

Prompt

What does returning let me see, and what remains unknown after the tree is in front of me again?

Field Notes

Cold air, blue sky, and sunlight behind the walnut. After several days away, I am looking again at a tree I have pictured many times in its absence.

The canopy remains mostly green. Yellow leaflets stand out among the green, and I photograph one close enough to see its surface. There seem to be more yellow leaves above and more fallen leaves below than at my previous visit. The comparison depends on what I remember.

Looking upward from my familiar position, I have the impression that more branches are visible. I cannot yet say how much of that impression belongs to changed foliage, today's light, or the expectation I brought with me. A few walnuts lie on the ground. I do not see any in the canopy from the positions I take this morning.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

October 18, 2026. The walnut's branching canopy against blue sky, with sunlight passing through foliage. This photograph records the return view; it does not establish when particular leaves fell.

Closer to the trunk, the bark holds my attention: deep grooves, rough edges, smoother stretches. Remembering that surface and standing before it are different encounters. Familiarity gives me reasons to look again.

I also think about a small piece of bark that came away from this tree last year and now sits on my desk. I looked at it last night. I've thought of it as a gift from the walnut, but that describes something about how I receive it, not an intention I can attribute to the tree. I didn't witness exactly how it came loose, and finding something detached isn't the same as being invited to take it. It's another way the history of this particular tree continues to matter.

Reflection

I had wondered what autumn would have changed by the time I returned. Some of what I expected now seems to be here. Nothing needs to have surprised me for the visit to matter.

There is a small but consequential distinction between seeing leaves on the ground and knowing their history. I can compare today's scene with a remembered one. I did not watch those particular leaves fall, and their presence does not tell me precisely when or why they detached. Likewise, the walnuts I cannot now see do not reveal what became of them.

Attention includes allowing an expectation to meet the scene without demanding either confirmation or a dramatic reversal. This morning offers detail and renewed presence, with several comparisons still tentative.

Remainder changes shape on returning. The anticipated view has become available, while the days between visits remain unobserved. Knowing this tree more intimately does not make its history transparent.

Research Connection

Husserl gives familiarity substantial philosophical weight. In Ideas II §59, his discussion of habitual capacities includes expectations shaped by earlier experience, sometimes before they become explicit. That account helps explain why I return already disposed to notice certain features. Renewed perception can confirm or qualify an expectation without requiring a new kind of intentionality.

Maurice Merleau-Ponty complicates the relation in another way. His late account of flesh makes noncoincidence part of sensible belonging: relation does not culminate in complete possession of what is encountered. Yet his distinction between world-flesh and self-sensing bodily flesh also prevents shared surroundings from becoming evidence that the walnut experiences this return as I do.

Edith Stein gives another question a place here. Her discussion of vegetal life allows a qualified apprehension of growth, vigor, or decline without granting me access to an awake vegetal consciousness or the cause of a particular change. These yellow leaflets don't establish how well this walnut is doing.

Robin Wall Kimmerer helps me examine the bark I've been calling a gift. In Braiding Sweetgrass, gratitude and reciprocity can change how a person receives the world without requiring a plant to have planned a present. That doesn't settle the question of whether collecting a piece of bark was appropriate. Availability isn't an invitation.

For Ecological Intentionality, the question remains whether the practice contributes something philosophically distinct or cultivates capacities these accounts already describe. Investigating this walnut's living processes and possible needs requires further evidence. The tree's particular life must matter to that inquiry even where my familiar view cannot supply the answer.

Question Carried Forward

What has renewed perception actually added to my knowledge of this walnut, and what further evidence would I need before making a claim about its life or its good?

item.title: When the Conditions Change
item.description: A colder coastal morning asks what changed conditions disclose and what the anticipated return to the walnut leaves open.
item.content:encoded:
October 17, 2026 · Black walnut practice, coastal comparison · approximately 25 minutes recorded

Prompt

What changes in an encounter when the weather changes, and what remains to be learned by returning?

Field Notes

The Atlantic lies beneath a broad clouded sky this morning. A narrow band of warm light remains near the horizon, and waves leave white edges along the shore. Yesterday's bright blue sky is something I remember while looking at this different scene.

The air feels colder. Wind makes itself felt against my skin, and I have added clothing and sought shelter. The change reaches me through more than the view. A few birds visit the balcony and look toward the interior, briefly interrupting the reflection. I cannot tell from that visit exactly what brought them here.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

October 17, 2026. Cloud cover over the Atlantic, with a thin band of warm light and breaking waves below. The photograph preserves the view; the felt cold belongs to the account of being there.

The walnut is elsewhere this morning. I am thinking ahead to the next encounter: whether its canopy will have changed, whether more leaves will be on the ground. Those possibilities are already directing my attention, although I have not yet seen what awaits.

Reflection

A conversation yesterday about intentionality has stayed with me. It made me notice how much I can anticipate an encounter before it happens, including what I expect it might mean. But those expectations are mine. The encounter may confirm them, complicate them, or turn my attention somewhere I hadn't expected.

I came outside expecting cooler weather. Now the expectation meets the particular feel of the morning. The forecast and the encounter have different roles: one prepared me for conditions; the other gives me wind, cold, light, and water from this bodily situation. Feeling the wind does not let me see the whole atmospheric system described by a weather map.

The anticipated return to the walnut brings another distinction into focus. A new view may confirm or complicate what I expect. Even if more leaves are down, I will not thereby have witnessed their falling or learned the precise causes of the change.

Remainder has a temporal shape here. Yesterday's brightness is remembered, today's cold is felt, and the walnut's next appearance is anticipated. Returning can change what is available without making the interval between visits transparent.

Research Connection

Husserl makes the philosophical question harder in a useful way. In Ideas II §18(b), changing illumination and other perceptual conditions already belong to the account of how the same thing appears differently. His resources extend beyond a perceiver walking around an object. Weather changing at a familiar standpoint gives no immediate reason to claim that a new kind of intentionality has been discovered.

Maurice Merleau-Ponty presses a further question about the perceiver's belonging to the sensible world. His later account of flesh includes divergence and incomplete reversibility: relation does not require complete coincidence. But my exposure to the wind cannot establish that ontology, and a shared sensible world does not mean that the ocean experiences the weather as I do.

For Ecological Intentionality, two tasks remain. First, what does late flesh explain beyond the already embodied and temporal accounts available in Husserl and early Merleau-Ponty? Then, what additional work does an ecological account perform? Understanding how conditions appear to me and investigating their consequences for particular living beings require connected but distinguishable inquiries. The need for both does not yet settle whether a new philosophical category is necessary.

Question Carried Forward

When I return to the walnut, what will actually revise my expectations, and what will remain unknown even after I can see the tree again?

item.title: No Line on the Horizon
item.description: A coastal comparison asks what distance and proximity disclose, and what further encounter leaves unknown.
item.content:encoded:
October 16, 2026 · Black walnut practice, coastal comparison · approximately 22 minutes recorded

Prompt

What becomes visible from a distance, what becomes available through proximity, and what does neither perspective establish?

Field Notes

This morning I carry the walnut practice to the coast. From a balcony, sunlight spreads across the Atlantic. Waves approach the shore in bands, foam gathers along their edges, and people move through a scene large enough to make them appear small. The horizon is sharply visible.

U2's “No Line on the Horizon” comes to mind. The title sits strangely beside the clarity of the line before me. I can see a boundary in this view without treating it as a physical seam between ocean and sky.

The balcony offers patterns that would be harder to take in from the sand. I am still bodily present here: feeling the air, facing the light, standing within a structure that makes this particular view possible.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

October 16, 2026. Morning sunlight across the Atlantic; the elevated view gathers horizon, breaking waves, and shoreline into one scene.

On the beach, the broad surface differentiates into shells and fragments. There are variations in size, shape, color, and texture; comparatively intact pieces lie among broken ones. Darker materials remain unidentified. Getting closer makes these differences available.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

October 16, 2026. Shells and fragments on the beach. Close examination brings individual forms into view without revealing how each came to be here.

Then I turn around and photograph the building. The balconies, railings, and windows occupy the scene I had been surveying. The place from which I looked has become something I can look at.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site.

October 16, 2026. Looking back toward the balconies from the sand. The building that made the elevated view possible becomes part of the visible scene.

Reflection

The movement between balcony and sand changes what I can describe. It also makes the limits of description more exact.

Close to the shells, I can distinguish fragments that disappeared into the larger view. I still do not know how long each has been here, where it came from, or what brought it to this stretch of beach. The lives of the organisms that produced them remain outside this morning's observation. More detail gives inquiry somewhere to begin.

Looking back at the building produces a similar distinction. Its visible structure helps me locate my earlier perspective. Its construction, maintenance, and histories of access require other evidence. Seeing where I stood does not disclose everything that made standing there possible.

This returns me to the walnut. A fallen branch can become easier to examine on the ground while its falling and previous condition remain unwitnessed. Attention gains precision when it can say what has become available and what question still needs another method.

Remainder changes with the encounter. A previously indistinct surface becomes differentiated; the history of its fragments remains unresolved. Neither distance nor proximity deserves an automatic claim to completeness. Even with a closer look, the origins of particular fragments might remain unrecoverable. A species identification, if I could establish one, would still differ from the history of this particular shell and the developmental possibilities of the life that produced it.

Research Connection

Husserl helps explain why moving matters. In Ideas II, his analysis of bodily movement describes how changes of orientation motivate changing appearances and open further possibilities of perception. Walking between viewpoints gives this account work to do. The visible ocean horizon and philosophical horizonality should nevertheless remain distinct: one belongs to the scene before me; the other concerns how an appearance refers beyond what is presently given.

Maurice Merleau-Ponty sharpens the question of belonging to the visible world. Looking back at the building makes the location of my earlier seeing part of what can be seen. His later account of flesh and incomplete reversibility invites a stronger inquiry into that belonging. The photograph alone cannot establish the ontology, and being affected by the ocean does not establish that the ocean experiences me. A further difficulty is that an elevated perspective isn't necessarily a deficient one. The value of moving closer depends on what I'm trying to understand; even the best available perspective leaves other questions unanswered.

For Ecological Intentionality, the task becomes more precise. A possible further view, an object's recoverable history, and the developmental possibilities of a living being call for different warrants. The discipline may lie in recognizing when one kind of inquiry has reached its limit and another needs to begin. Whether that requires a new philosophical category remains open.

The line on the horizon is still there. Having moved between perspectives, I have more to describe and more exact questions to ask.

Question Carried Forward

When a new perspective reveals something I couldn't previously see, what knowledge have I gained, and what would I still need to investigate before claiming to understand the encounter?

item.title: What Changes the Next Question?
item.description: A fallen leaf opens a question about origin and what inquiry should do next.
item.content:encoded:
October 15, 2026 · Black walnut · approximately 22 minutes recorded

Prompt

When a judgment changes, what happens to the question I ask next?

Field Notes

Another sunny morning beneath the walnut. Birds are loud nearby. Green and yellow leaves catch the light overhead, and the familiar photograph requires a small adjustment. Over recent mornings, I have shifted from my usual position to keep the sun behind the trunk. The changing light becomes noticeable partly through where I need to stand.

The birds interrupt my usual focus on the tree. At 8:42, Cornell's Merlin Bird ID suggests Northern Cardinal, Carolina Wren, Blue Jay, Carolina Chickadee, Eastern Phoebe, Mourning Dove, and House Finch from sound. I hear birds, but the app's list isn't seven independently confirmed sightings. Merlin itself describes Sound ID results as suggestions to compare with recordings. Identifying a voice isn't yet locating an individual bird or establishing its relation to this walnut.

Looking toward the ground, I take a fallen leaf to have come from this walnut. Then I pause over the attribution. Being beneath the tree is not enough to establish its origin. There are other trees nearby, including other walnuts. Recognizing a leaf's kind would not necessarily tell me which individual tree produced it.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site. October 15, 2026. Sunlight behind the trunk, with green and yellow foliage against blue sky.

Photograph available on the illustrated field-notes site. October 15, 2026. A closer view into the branching canopy and compound leaves. This photograph records foliage rather than the origin of a particular fallen leaf or the birds heard nearby.

Reflection

A familiar place can invite an explanation before I have noticed what supports it. The leaf fits the story I expect from an autumn morning. That makes the story plausible; it does not give me the leaf's particular history.

I consider looking more closely at shape, veins, and the distinction between a leaf and a leaflet. The question remains open this morning. I cannot yet tell a story about discovering that my first judgment was wrong.

Still, the possibility matters. If another origin were established, I might correct the description and stop there. Or I might begin asking how material from neighboring plants arrives here. That second question would need its own observations. Imagining it does not establish the relationship.

The birds pose a related test that I hadn't planned for today's leaf exercise. Listening is one mode of encounter; identifying calls through a trained application adds a tool and a source of possible error. Checking a suggestion may require listening again, locating the bird, or comparing another recording. The next question is partly shaped by the methods available to me, not only by the tree I intended to study.

Attention includes allowing a familiar account to become questionable. Remainder here is quite specific: a visible specimen whose origin remains unsettled. Looking more carefully may help with identification without recovering its unwitnessed journey.

Research Connection

Husserl makes the next step harder to claim as something new. In Ideas II, §55, he describes how what appears can motivate comparison, closer inspection, and action. He also allows the surrounding world to become a theme for scientific investigation and deliberation about goals. His account has room for more than replacing one judgment with another.

This puts pressure on Ecological Intentionality. If the practice changes what I investigate, that may be an education of capacities already available within intentional life. It does not by itself establish a new structure. The task is to follow an actual change closely enough to say what prompted it, what evidence it needs, and what remains unresolved.

For now, the leaf's origin remains a question. It need not supply a philosophical breakthrough to deserve a more careful description.
